Tech Report: Where is freshwater wildlife under the most pressure? A newly introduced map offers surprises

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1058 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A global study maps 45 threats to 21,490 freshwater species and reveals where conservation looks based on land wildlife can miss areas of high risk.
  • Rivers, lakes and wetlands are home to nearly a third of all known vertebrate species.
  • A fresh global study maps where 45 human pressures, from crop farming to dam construction, are most likely to affect freshwater wildlife.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A global study maps 45 threats to 21,490 freshwater species and reveals where conservation looks based on land wildlife can miss areas of high risk.

Rivers, lakes and wetlands are home to nearly a third of all known vertebrate species.

A fresh global study maps where 45 human pressures, from crop farming to dam construction, are most likely to affect freshwater wildlife.

A team led from McGill University analyzed 21,490 species and found that freshwater threat hotspots often differ from those on land.

For the threats compared, freshwater mammals generally faced greater pressure than land mammals, with a smaller gap for reptiles.

Christophe Brabant, a doctoral student in biology at McGill University, led the work with biology professor Lars Lønsmann Iversen, a member of McGill’s Bieler School of Environment.

The researchers drew on expert assessments to identify the threats facing each species.

They combined those assessments with species’ known ranges to map where the threats are most likely to affect them.

The researchers identified three threats that were especially widespread.

Sources indicate that across river sub-basins worldwide, they estimated that each affected roughly one in four freshwater species present, on average. Farmland growing crops came first.

Dams and other water management came second, and runoff from farms and forestry third.

Europe and northwestern Africa’s Maghreb region carry the heaviest combined load of all 45 threats. In Europe, the dominant problem is pollution from cities, farms and industry.

Sources indicate that in the Maghreb it is pollution plus dams and heavy water use. Other hot spots include the Nile, the Niger Delta and the Rift Valley lakes of East Africa.

The lightest loads are where few people live, in Siberia and northern Canada, and in the Sahara, Arabian and Australian deserts.

It has been revealed that global averages hide massive differences between animals. Fish are mainly hit by fishing across 37% of their range and by dams across another 30.5%.

Farming was the leading threat across 45.8% of amphibians’ combined range and 31.45% of the combined range of dragonflies and damselflies.

The authors linked this pattern to the animals’ reliance on both land and water at different stages of life.

Freshwater reptiles and mammals face a different enemy. Hunting and other direct use are the main threat across 37.8% of reptile ranges and 43.4% of mammal ranges.

That covers the wildlife trade, traditional medicine, animals caught in fishing gear and animals killed on purpose.

In an interview with Earth.com, Brabant noted that dams, farmland, and farm pollution are widespread, but their weight changes from region to region and group to group.

“This means there is no one-size-fits-all approach to freshwater conservation,” he said.

The raw material was the Red List kept by the International Union for Conservation of Nature, which records for each assessed species the threats experts have seen affecting it.

The team took five groups that have been assessed in full: amphibians, fish, mammals, reptiles, and the dragonflies and damselflies.

For each species, they combined its range map with its threat list.

“By combining this data, we could calculate, for any sub-watershed, the probability that a species occurring there is affected by a particular threat,” Brabant noted.

One map per threat per group made 225 maps, which the team stacked into a single index of combined pressure.

Species with small ranges were given more weight.

A threat recorded for a species found in one lake can be placed on the map with confidence, while one recorded for a species spread across a continent can’t.

To test whether the maps mean anything for survival, the team compared them with two separate records.

In the 5% of river basins where extinction risk is modeled to be highest, 71% of the 45 threats were more likely to affect a species than their global average.

The second record was the Living Planet Index, which tracks counts of individual animal populations over time.

Across 2,568 freshwater vertebrate populations from 600 species, populations were shrinking faster in basins with a heavier combined threat load.

Neither record was used to build the maps, so the match is not circular.

The authors wrote that it suggests the maps capture where threats are already pushing freshwater species toward decline.

The study also lined up the freshwater maps against earlier ones made the same way for land vertebrates.

For all seven threats that had been mapped on land, freshwater mammals were more likely to be affected than land mammals.

Freshwater reptiles revealed the same pattern with a smaller gap, which the authors put down to the time reptiles still spend on land.

The hot spots were in different places, too. Where freshwater fish and frogs are under the most pressure is not where land vertebrates are.

“What surprised me most was how different the geography was,” Brabant told Earth.com. Conservation planning has often relied on information about land species, he noted.

That is why freshwater species and their threats need to be written into aims explicitly if the plans are going to reach them.

The Red List treats each threat as if it acted alone, and the authors wrote that many of them combine in ways that could make the damage worse.

The maps estimate how likely species are to be affected in each area. They don’t measure how much harm each threat causes.

Range maps describe where species live today, so places a threat has already emptied may not show up.

Industry observers note that asked which places he would look at first, Brabant said threat alone isn’t enough. Europe and northwestern Africa lead on accumulated threats, while many tropical regions stand out for the number of species affected.

“Areas of high richness and high threat suggest that threat mitigation is most urgent, whereas areas of high richness and low threats would be most suitable for proactive protection,” he mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that what would help most right now, he said, is reducing the pressures: cleaner water, protected habitat and rivers reconnected. But the most useful action depends on the place and the species.

The next step is matching each basin’s threats to the conservation actions that address them, which the maps alone can’t do yet.

The full study was published in the journal Science.

How the ‘blue tsunami’ crested in North Carolina

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1621 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, north Carolina Rep.-elect LaKesha Womack talks to reporters Sunday at the AC Hotel in Washington as she arrives for new member orientation.
  • LaKesha Womack faced towering odds as an underfunded Democrat making her first run for public office in a North Carolina district that Donald Trump carried by 15 points two years ago.
  • Industry observers note that but as early voting surged in mid-October, she sensed she might pull off an upset over Republican Rep.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, north Carolina Rep.-elect LaKesha Womack talks to reporters Sunday at the AC Hotel in Washington as she arrives for new member orientation. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

LaKesha Womack faced towering odds as an underfunded Democrat making her first run for public office in a North Carolina district that Donald Trump carried by 15 points two years ago.

Industry observers note that but as early voting surged in mid-October, she sensed she might pull off an upset over Republican Rep. Tim Moore, the influential former speaker of the North Carolina House and a chief architect of the gerrymander that aimed to keep the 14th District safely red.

According to recent reports, “There were a lot of pins and needles,” said Womack, a 49-year-old ordained minister who works at a Charlotte-based nonprofit. After seeing long lines at polling places extend into Election Day, she grew more confident: “People were ready to exercise their voice.”.

Womack – who raised less than $60,000 to Moore’s $2.1 million – eked out a 2-point win in the district, which reaches from the Charlotte suburbs to mountain counties in the west.

Saddled with an unpopular president and broad dissatisfaction with the status quo, Republican incumbents across the nation experienced a midterm drubbing last week. As of Monday evening, House Democrats had netted 42 seats, with more races left to be called. The GOP in North Carolina, a state that Trump carried three times, was among the hardest hit.

Democrats have so far flipped five House seats in the Tar Heel State. Besides Womack, the “blue tsunami” also swept in Paul Barringer, a lawyer who founded an outdoor clothing line, and High Point Mayor Cyril Jefferson. And Army veteran Richard Ojeda, who once served in the West Virginia Senate, defeated Rep. Richard Hudson, the chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee.

According to recent reports, democrats also won two races that had been seen as competitive for much of the cycle. Farmer Jamie Ager flipped an open seat in the state’s mountain west, while Rep. Don Davis held on to his Eastern North Carolina district, which Republicans had redrawn in their favor.

Meanwhile, in the state’s hilly northwest corner, 11-term Republican Virginia Foxx, the chairwoman of the powerful Rules Committee, is fighting for her political future: As of Monday afternoon, former journalist Chuck Hubbard led her by 99 votes in the 5th District, though The Associated Press had yet to call the race.

That was also true in the neighboring 10th District, where GOP incumbent Pat Harrigan had a 1-point edge over Democratic physician associate Ashley Bell. Also uncalled were a pair of contests in Eastern North Carolina, where Republican Rep. Greg Murphy clung to a 233-vote edge over Democratic former state Rep. Raymond Smith and GOP Rep. David Rouzer led Democratic social worker Kimberly Hardy by less than a point.

“Nobody could have predicted this,’’ mentioned David Wilson Brown, who leads the Democratic Party in Gaston County near Charlotte and has lost two bids for the House, including to Foxx in 2020. “It’s a watershed moment.”.

The Democratic rout in the midterm elections was powered by victories in states with latest GOP-favored maps, including Texas, Ohio and Florida.

Industry observers note that but Democrats’ success in North Carolina was especially striking given the steep structural disadvantages the party faced. Since Republicans flipped the state legislature in 2010, and with it control of the redistricting process, no House GOP incumbent had lost a general election in the Tar Heel State until last week.

This year’s  congressional map – the state's sixth in seven election cycles – was engineered by the Republican-led legislature to help the party capture 11 of the state's 14 House seats.

Sources indicate that but the Democratic surge was so big that it easily overpowered the GOP’s built-in edge. Democratic candidates were also lifted by former Gov. Roy Cooper, whose 20-point Senate win provided the underticket with powerful coattails.

According to recent reports, “In order for them to gerrymander our state in the way that they did, they were spread very thin,” Brown said, referring to state Republicans. “So they were kind of ripe to be defeated that way.”.

The repeated rounds of redistricting may have also erased some of the advantages of incumbency, according to Peter L. Francia, a political science professor at East Carolina University. “If you carve up a district every two years, you've taken away some of that [advantage]. And I think that that came back and hurt Republicans in this cycle.”.

Doug Heye, a GOP strategist and a former spokesman for the Republican National Committee, said redistricting “ticked off a whole lot of voters, and really activated the Democratic base.”.

On the Republican side, voters were “less motivated because they were unexcited about Trump,’’ Heye added.

Republican incumbents accustomed to winning by comfortable margins weren’t prepared for a political environment driven by anger over the war in Iran and angst about the rising cost of living.

It has been revealed that “Clearly, a lot of those Republicans didn’t take their elections seriously,” Heye said. “They won last time with 18 points. They weren't on anyone's radar screen, so they didn't think they had to do anything.”.

Womack credits her win to a grassroots campaign centered on economic issues. While her race wasn’t on the national radar – Moore, after all, won by 16 points in 2024 – and her campaign didn’t have money for ads, she was out in the district doing events every day.

It has been revealed that “There are a lot of working families right now who are in the missing middle,” she noted in an interview. “They make too much money to get help, but they don't make enough money to get ahead. … Someone who can be working a full-time job, but still doesn’t have enough money to buy groceries or to afford their medications or to have access to health insurance.”.

It has been revealed that womack remarked her own struggles have shaped her approach to politics. This week, she’s slated to appear in court on a felony charge for allegedly failing to return a rental car in 2019. The incident wound up in one of Moore’s attack ads.

“There are so many people who [understand] what happens when you're down on your luck and you don't have enough money to make good financial decisions,’’ she said. “Most people don't want those bad decisions to be a definition of their character for the rest of their life.”.

Early in the midterm cycle, Democratic opposition research group American Bridge prepared detailed dossiers on Republican House incumbents in North Carolina.

“Someone like Virginia Foxx, she’s been on the Hill forever,” said Pat Dennis, the group’s president. “She was somebody … who under the radar could be vulnerable. So we started really early.”.

American Bridge’s political arm spent $340,000 on ads targeting Foxx. One spot featured a man who identified himself as a Trump voter expressing anger at the government’s response to Hurricane Helene, which devastated the mountain communities of Western North Carolina two years ago.

Other Democrats scoffed at the group’s decision to spend money targeting entrenched Republicans far from the main House battleground.

“There was a lot of reluctance from people to really believe that that data was correct, but it was,’’ Dennis stated. “Then over the summer, we saw her numbers collapsing, so we put paid media behind it and it really paid off.”.

Hubbard ran against Foxx two years ago and lost by almost 20 points.

It has been revealed that “I kind of had a notion I was going to do this again,’’ he said in an interview Saturday while en route to Washington for freshman orientation. “I don’t like to lose at checkers, much less a congressional race.”.

After a court-drawn map resulted in a split North Carolina delegation after the 2022 elections, state Republicans won back control of the map-making process and went on to win 10 of the state’s 14 House seats under a new map two years later.

At Trump’s urging, Republicans made further tweaks to the North Carolina map last year, but the original gerrymander finally came back to bite the GOP in 2026, according to Hubbard.

“North Carolina is one of the most severely gerrymandered states,’’ he remarked. “And what happened was they had to steal from Peter to pay Paul. It's been referred to by political scientists as a dummymander.”.

As the vote count in the 5th District continues, Foxx, whose campaign declined to comment for this story, has requested the presence of nonpartisan election observers.

They “will serve as key, watchful eyes to ensure that this sacred process is not impeded and that all legal votes are counted in a consistent, thorough manner,’’ she posted on social media.

But even before the final races are called, Republicans are already looking to the next election.

Heye, who expects North Carolina to remain a purple state in 2028 and beyond, cautioned the Democrats who won last week not to get too comfortable in Washington. He invoked Fred Heineman, the former Raleigh police chief who rode the 1994 “Republican Revolution” to Congress – and lasted a single term.

“Some of them will lose, and some of the people who lost may run two years from now and get their seat back,’’ he said.

One GOP operative, who requested anonymity to speak candidly, offered up a similar assessment.

Trump “didn't keep his promises” and that “just got voters very angry and suppressed the GOP base from coming out because, in a midterm election it's a base turnout contest,’’ the strategist said.

“But these Democrats are renting these districts for two years.”.

Why does Webb see so many giant galaxies in the early universe?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1107 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Lumina simulation traces how stars and quasars transformed gas in the early universe and explores why Webb sees so many massive galaxies.
  • The first stars and galaxies gave off ultraviolet light that stripped electrons from hydrogen atoms between galaxies.
  • Quasars later began stripping helium of its last electron, a process that took more energetic light and was still underway long after most of the hydrogen had been ionized.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Lumina simulation traces how stars and quasars transformed gas in the early universe and explores why Webb sees so many massive galaxies.

The first stars and galaxies gave off ultraviolet light that stripped electrons from hydrogen atoms between galaxies.

Quasars later began stripping helium of its last electron, a process that took more energetic light and was still underway long after most of the hydrogen had been ionized.

A newly introduced computer simulation called Lumina tracks how gas, dark matter and light interacted through both changes.

It models a region that would span about 1.6 billion light-years on each side at today’s cosmic scale, giving astronomers a way to test their predictions against observations from the James Webb Space Telescope.

Oliver Zier, a fellow at the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian, led the project.

Aaron Smith of the University of Texas at Dallas was a co-author, along with colleagues at MIT, York University and the Max Planck Institute for Astrophysics.

Industry observers note that “With JWST, the early universe has become an exciting upcoming frontier in astrophysics,” Zier noted. “To understand what we are seeing with this telescope, we need to translate our theories into detailed predictions.”.

Sources indicate that A simulation is that translation. Astronomers feed in the laws of physics and the universe’s starting conditions, then let a supercomputer calculate how everything develops over time.

They compare the result with real telescope images. A match gives astronomers more confidence in the model. A mismatch can show where its assumptions need more testing.

Lumina covers roughly the first 2 billion years, following the earliest galaxies and the thin gas between them.

The simulated cube is about 1.6 billion light-years on a side, more than 100 times the volume of comparable simulations.

The team divided its contents into 432 billion pieces of gas and dark matter, and each piece of gas has about 3.6 million times the mass of the Sun.

Galaxies grow where the dark matter gathers, strung along the filaments of the cosmic web.

The team ran Lumina on Frontier, a supercomputer at Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee.

The simulation used 7,536 graphics accelerators, just over 20% of the machine, and about 600 terabytes of working memory at its peak.

Smith described what that size makes possible.

“For the first time, we can follow along as both hydrogen and helium changed into their modern form across such an enormous volume of the universe, while still resolving the galaxies and other luminous objects driving that transformation,” he noted.

Sources indicate that earlier simulations of this kind, including the Thesan project, stopped before helium began to clear. Lumina’s cube is 144 times the volume of Thesan’s.

The first stars and galaxies cleared the hydrogen slowly and unevenly. In Lumina, bubbles of cleared gas open around the biggest galaxies first and grow until they merge. Regions far from any galaxy stay foggy longest.

The team divided the simulation into 125 regions and tracked how swiftly the hydrogen changed in each one.

Sources indicate that in a typical region, nearly all of the hydrogen gas between galaxies had lost its electrons by about 1.1 billion years after the Substantial Bang. In the slowest regions, that took about 1.3 billion years.

Astronomers see the same late finish in the light of distant quasars, which still highlights absorption by hydrogen gas at that time.

According to recent reports, stars did nearly all of this work. Quasars supplied about 15% of the hydrogen-clearing light near the end.

Recent findings suggest that clearing helium takes light about four times more energetic than clearing hydrogen, and ordinary stars give off very little of it. Quasars do.

A quasar is a supermassive black hole pulling in gas so fast that the gas shines with intense ultraviolet light.

In Lumina, the brightest quasars began stripping helium of its last electron about 900 million years after the Massive Bang. The process was about halfway complete by 1.5 billion years.

By 2 billion years, the regions where helium still held its last electron accounted for less than 1% of the space Lumina modeled.

The bubbles around quasars grew larger than the hydrogen bubbles that formed around galaxies.

Industry observers note that each clearing also heats the gas. The thin gas between galaxies warms to roughly 18,000°F to 36,000°F (10,000°C to 20,000°C) while the hydrogen clears.

It cools as the universe expands, then warms again when the quasar light reaches it.

Recent findings suggest that measurements of the helium clearing are scarce. Most studies of it rely on fewer than about 25 quasars with a usable line of sight, and Lumina’s timing agrees with those measurements.

Lumina also grows galaxies, and here it fails a test. At about 1.2 billion years after the Big Bang and earlier, the simulation produces fewer very massive galaxies than Webb has found.

The shortfall grows the further back in time the comparison goes.

The team wrote that this confirms a known problem: galaxy models tuned to the nearby universe undercount the giants Webb sees in the early one.

Stars might form more efficiently in the earliest substantial galaxies, or the masses astronomers read off Webb’s images might be less certain than assumed.

The simulation can’t settle that on its own, but it marks where the standard picture falls short.

Some of Lumina’s agreement with observations is built in.

It has been revealed that the authors set the share of each galaxy’s hydrogen-clearing light that escapes into space at 18%, a value chosen so that hydrogen clears on a realistic schedule. So the timing of that clearing is partly a tuning choice, not a prediction.

The team also slowed the speed of light in the calculation to a fifth of its real value, because the full speed would have made the run unaffordable.

That shortcut may keep hydrogen fog in remote voids a little too long. And the detailed comparison with real quasar spectra, the one that would say whether the helium timing is right, is still to come.

Zier’s team looks to release the full Lumina data in 2028. Companion studies are already using it to work out how patchy clearing marks the afterglow of the Big Bang, and how many quasars of each brightness the early universe held.

Observations from Webb and future surveys by the Roman Space Telescope will help astronomers test whether Lumina can explain how the earliest massive galaxies formed.

The full study was published in the journal Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society.

Two stars in the Andromeda galaxy merged before astronomers’ eyes

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (459 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • According to recent reports, for seven years, a giant star in the Andromeda galaxy grew brighter.
  • According to recent reports, in work published last year, after poring through nearly 30 years of telescope data, astronomers had found that the giant began brightening in 2018 and proposed that a smaller star was circling ever closer around a giant companion and had even slipped inside its outermost layers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

According to recent reports, for seven years, a giant star in the Andromeda galaxy grew brighter. It swelled to more than twice its original size, even as its surface temperature barely changed. Then, in October 2025, it erupted. The slow brightening and sudden eruption tell a story of a smaller star orbiting inside of a massive star and what became of the pair, researchers report November 18 in Nature.

According to recent reports, in work published last year, after poring through nearly 30 years of telescope data, astronomers had found that the giant began brightening in 2018 and proposed that a smaller star was circling ever closer around a giant companion and had even slipped inside its outermost layers. Astronomers call this elusive phase of a binary star’s life common-envelope evolution.

Now, the astronomers have analyzed the system’s dramatic next developments, culminating in the October 2025 eruption. (The stars are nicknamed Little Bao and Significant Bao as a nod to that event’s official designation, AT 2025abao.).

First, astrophysicist Viraj Karambelkar of Columbia University and colleagues revisited those years of brightening given the imminent eruption. One cause of the brightening could have been gas flowing away from the stars, giving off light as it slowed down. But even if all the energy of that moving gas turned into light, it still wouldn’t be enough to explain the glow.

Instead, the researchers determined that the binary hypothesis they had originally proposed fit better: As Little Bao orbited inside Big Bao’s gas outer layers, the gas pushed back against the little star. That drag made Little Bao spiral inward and transfer energy to the surrounding gas. Some of that energy escaped as light, making Big Bao shine brighter.

Industry observers note that then, it was time to dig into what caused the eruption. If the outburst threw enough of the shared gas into space, the individual stars could have survived in an even tighter orbit. But the team estimates that only about a tenth of the giant’s outer gas escaped. The energy carried by that fast-moving gas also suggests that Little Bao reached Big Bao’s core. Together, those clues point to a merger.

Still, too much dust clouds the system to directly see what remains. And it won’t settle for years or even decades, although Karambelkar and his colleagues will be watching.

In a recent development, they’ll be looking for more examples of this type of merger, too. “Now we can go and try to look for similar systems,” Karambelkar says, “and hopefully aim to catch more of these systems even before they erupt.”.

You Can Build All the Power Plants You Want. Without This Overlooked Machine, None of Them Will Matter.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that as humanity entered the 21st century and the ravages of climate change became more and more apparent, the push toward electrification (replacing gas-powered cars, furnaces, and stoves with electric versions) really gained steam.
  • But building out an electrified future isn’t as easy as sticking wind turbines in the ocean and vast solar arrays in the desert and calling it a day.
  • In a new study published in the journal Cell Reports Sustainability, researchers at Johns Hopkins University report that critical grid equipment, such as transformers and converters, could become the bottleneck in powering a rapidly electrifying society.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that as humanity entered the 21st century and the ravages of climate change became more and more apparent, the push toward electrification (replacing gas-powered cars, furnaces, and stoves with electric versions) really gained steam. At the same time, the electricity supply itself has been getting cleaner. According to Pew Research, solar power accounted for only 0.01 percent of the world’s electricity production back then, but fast-forward a quarter of a century, and that number is now nine percent and rising.

But building out an electrified future isn’t as easy as sticking wind turbines in the ocean and vast solar arrays in the desert and calling it a day. These new forms of renewable energy also need to connect to the grid before they can supply us with that much-needed new power. Expanding the grid’s capacity to meet this ballooning demand was already going to be a tall order as more and more electric cars, ovens, and heat pumps came online. Now, the rise of power-hungry AI data centers has transformed that difficult task into a borderline impossible one for the simple reason that the U.S. may not have enough of the equipment—or the materials to make said equipment—to build the required infrastructure.

In a new study published in the journal Cell Reports Sustainability, researchers at Johns Hopkins University report that critical grid equipment, such as transformers and converters, could become the bottleneck in powering a rapidly electrifying society. According to the researchers, demand for electricity isn’t anything new. In fact, it’s been steadily rising since Thomas Edison flipped the switch on the Pearl Street Station in 1882. But due to the rise of AI data centers, the electricity industry has entered a whole new era of demand growth.

“When the demand for electricity started to grow faster than expected, it started to amplify all the cracks in the industry,” Yury Dvorkin, a Johns Hopkins researcher and co-author of the study, mentioned in a press statement. According to Dvorkin and co-author Boyu Yao, electricity demand historically ticked up a percent or two each year. But now, largely because of data centers, demand is projected to grow 21 percent overall by the end of the decade.

If this rapid demand growth persists, it will put considerable strain on supplies of specific materials, including copper, steel, nickel, aluminum, and manganese, needed to build the necessary transformers, which step up or step down the voltage of alternating current on the grid.

“This type of equipment was taken for granted, but without it, you can build a data center or a power plant but it won’t be powered because you cannot connect it to the grid,” Dvorkin said. “By 2030 we’re likely to have transformer shortages even without the most aggressive power demand growth.”.

According to their projections, copper will run short in 2027, followed soon by steel and nickel, which will affect not just grid utilities but wind power infrastructure and electric vehicle charging stations. This shortfall isn’t necessarily news: a study by S&P Global earlier this year found that copper could experience a 10 million metric ton deficit by 2040. This deficit isn’t caused by a lack of copper in the ground, since the planet holds abundant copper resources. Extraction is where the industry is facing a crucial bottleneck.

In a recent development, “Copper is abundant in the ground, but there’s not enough being extracted to be able to meet the demand,” authors of a copper market analysis wrote for The Conversation earlier this year. That’s because investors want higher and more reliable returns than copper mines at the moment offer, and the industry faces complex permitting processes and can’t find enough workers.

In a recent development, this latest study suggests that under its baseline scenario, the U.S. might be able to produce enough transformers yet still fall 16 percent short on other grid-related equipment. But with AI data centers supercharging demand, the study’s “high power demand” scenario is more likely. That scenario projects a 15 percent shortage of transformers and a 30 percent shortage of all other equipment. The authors also note that roughly two-thirds of this expected shortage can be attributed to AI data centers.

“Utilities will compete for transformers with the data center industry,” Dvorkin said. “Transformers will first be delivered to whoever can pay the highest premium. Will it be a mom-and-pop utility or a significant data center corporation?”.

I think we already know the answer to that question.

#65765. Industry News: The wildlife trade is bigger than previously thought, with nearly 80,000 species and counting

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1375 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: The wildlife trade is bigger than previously thought, with nearly 80,000 species and counting

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1375 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new review finds that global wildlife trade reaches far beyond familiar pets and seafood, and gaps in recordkeeping make its full scale hard to measure.
  • Recent findings suggest that ask about the wildlife trade and most people picture smuggled ivory, tiger skins and pangolins.
  • Most documented wildlife trade is legal, and it includes the fish in the freezer aisle, the orchid on the windowsill, and the gecko in the pet shop window.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new review finds that global wildlife trade reaches far beyond familiar pets and seafood, and gaps in recordkeeping make its full scale hard to measure.

Recent findings suggest that ask about the wildlife trade and most people picture smuggled ivory, tiger skins and pangolins. Almost none of the recorded trade is like that.

Most documented wildlife trade is legal, and it includes the fish in the freezer aisle, the orchid on the windowsill, and the gecko in the pet shop window.

A upcoming review documented 79,554 species in international wildlife trade, well above the roughly 50,000 previously estimated.

A broader tally that included species people use for subsistence and other purposes reached 107,356.

Even the new number is likely a considerable underestimate, the authors wrote, because almost no country records what it buys and sells.

Alice Hughes, a conservation scientist at the University of Melbourne, led the review. Her co-authors come from the organizations that track wildlife trade, including TRAFFIC, the IUCN and the UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization.

The count comes from stitching together databases built for other purposes, and the plant half of it rests on records of use rather than records of sale.

In an interview with Earth.com, Hughes said the finding is about ordinary buyers as much as smugglers.

“Almost all of us are part of wildlife trade, and whilst some of that, such as fisheries are managed, sectors like the pet trade are not,” she said.

Industry observers note that legal wildlife trade is worth an estimated $220 billion to $300 billion a year. Smuggled wildlife is worth an estimated $28 billion to $40 billion.

So the legal side is roughly six to 11 times larger than the smuggling that gets the attention.

Recent findings suggest that “When we think of wildlife trade we tend to think about the illegal trade of elephants, tigers and pangolins. But it’s much more than that,” Hughes mentioned.

“Wildlife trade includes everything from timber, seafood and medicinal plants to pets, cut flowers, ornamental fish and fungi, and most of it is legal.”.

Legal doesn’t mean harmless. Where researchers have population numbers for a traded species, the populations being collected from are, on average, 50% to 60% smaller than populations left alone.

By one estimate the authors cite, trade has contributed, directly or indirectly, to the global extinction of 294 species.

The team pulled together every trade record it could reach. The largest was the CITES Trade Database, which holds the records of legal trade in protected species going back to 1975.

Alongside it went the IUCN Red List, UN fish and timber records, TRAFFIC’s seizure reports and the US import database.

Beyond the databases, the researchers drew on published surveys of individual animal groups and a world checklist of plants that people use.

According to recent reports, animals accounted for 47,685 species, and up to 31,306 of those are vertebrates. That works out to 42% of every vertebrate species science has described.

Put another way, two out of every five kinds of animal with a backbone have been traded somewhere.

For birds, the share is higher still: about 65% of all living bird species have been traded. Plants and fungi added 59,671 species potentially used or traded.

Sources indicate that the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service logs wild animal shipments into and out of the United States in a database called LEMIS, and it periodically releases the records.

Since 2000, more than 21,000 wild animal species have been traded into the US alone.

According to recent reports, more than a quarter of all traded animal species appear in that one country’s records and in no other database. For mammals, the figure is 54%.

Much of what the world knows about which animals are traded comes from one country’s import records.

It has been revealed that hughes’s team surveyed 61 countries and searched for “wildlife trade database” in 30 languages. The US system was the only full, public record of trade across groups of animals from any country.

“The United States is the only country that systematically records and publicly shares trade data across a wide range of taxa. For much of the rest of the world, equivalent data simply does not exist,” Hughes mentioned.

Asked what it would take for other countries to follow, Hughes told Earth.com it starts with accepting that “legal trade is not necessarily sustainable.”.

Without data on trade in other groups, she said, the trade can’t be managed to make sure it is sustainable.

“Trade has changed, the exotic pet trade will continue to grow, and with so many species in trade, that poses a real risk unless we start monitoring it better,” she said.

In a recent development, the pet trade is where the new counts diverge most from the old global estimates. The gaps are largest for reptiles, invertebrates and plants, which are also the hardest to track.

A lizard or a beetle bought online travels by mail and often isn’t identified to species at the border.

Industry observers note that CITES, the treaty that regulates trade in at-risk species, covers about 9.5% of reptile species. The new review recorded 4,620 reptile species in trade, about 37% of all described reptiles.

Asked which traded species surprised her most, Hughes said it was how quickly newly described species appear for sale.

Collectors sometimes use the scientific descriptions themselves to find animals to trade, she said. She also pointed to “the price people are willing to pay for some, like 100s of dollars for a single isopod (woodlouse).”.

For buyers, Hughes said the place to start is where an animal came from.

Corn snakes and leopard geckos should be captive bred, she mentioned, and chameleons often come from the wild and don’t survive well in captivity.

“If you are not sure where they come from, just don’t buy them, for every wild caught animal in the shop, many others die in transit,” she mentioned.

Governments have agreed on a set of global biodiversity targets, and one of them covers the impacts of trade.

Recent findings suggest that its single headline measure is the share of fish stocks being fished at sustainable levels. By the review’s count, that measure reflects about 2% of the species in use and trade.

“While the global biodiversity framework does have a target on trade, based on our estimates it only accounts for around two or three percent of species in trade and misses the other 97 percent,” Hughes noted.

The authors wrote that the fix doesn’t need a upcoming system. Almost every country already runs customs checks and animal health checks on imports, and most CITES permits are still paper.

Electronic permits exist, but only about 30 of the 184 CITES countries use them.

If customs offices digitized shipping invoices and matched them to a species list, the authors wrote, they would record much of what is now lost.

The United Kingdom has required an electronic tag on every sheep, and a log of its movements, since 2009, so record-keeping on that scale is already being done.

Seizure records reflect how hard a country enforces its laws as much as how much is smuggled. And the databases don’t agree with one another on which species are traded, which is part of the paper’s point.

Even so, Hughes noted the estimate is still an underestimate, because most countries do not collect the data.

Recent findings suggest that the larger question is whether wild populations can sustain the trade. An IUCN working group has assessed the potential sustainability of trade for 347 species across 117 countries.

For many traded species, researchers still lack the data to tell how much is being taken from the wild and how those populations are faring.

Hughes and her co-authors propose standardizing how trade data are collected and starting at a regional level, with the European Union as a possible first model.

Until that happens, each upcoming database that opens is likely to add species to the count.

For many species, researchers still can’t tell how trade is affecting wild populations.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

Madrid 5-Day Itinerary: A Guide to Culture, Gastronomy, and Local Life

📅 06 May 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2458 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nomadicmatt

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, home to some 3.5 million people, Madrid is the capital of Spain and the country’s largest city.
  • In a recent development, like Barcelona, Madrid is a city that starts late and goes slow.
  • I’ve been a few times over the years and the city never ceases to amaze me.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, home to some 3.5 million people, Madrid is the capital of Spain and the country’s largest city. Though it’s somewhat sprawling, the city boasts stunning architecture, incredible food, and an energetic nightlife that stretches until dawn. Over 10 million people visit the city each year, and the minute you step out to explore, you’ll understand why Madrid is one of Europe’s top destinations.

In a recent development, like Barcelona, Madrid is a city that starts late and goes slow. It’s a city for night owls, where dinner starts late and the parties even later. But if you can embrace the laid-back pace of life, the slow meals, and the late-night vibes, you’ll have a more authentic visit and uncover the true beating heart of the city’s culture.

I love all my visits to Madrid. I’ve been a few times over the years and the city never ceases to amaze me. The food, the energy, the art (so much art!). Madrid is just cool.

Sources indicate that being such a big city, I know it can be easy to feel lost. Where do you start with what you want to do? Where do you go? It took me a few visits to figure it out.

In this post, I’ll help you plan an epic five-day visit to Madrid that will ensure you not only see the main sights but that you also get off the beaten path and see just what makes Madrid so popular — and all without breaking the bank either!

It has been revealed that this first day focuses on a prestigious area designated as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2021. There are over 40 monuments and over 40 buildings on the site. It’s easily one of the most picturesque and historic areas of the city.

Sources indicate that the route begins at the Prado Museum, one of the best museums on the planet. Here you’ll find works from El Greco, Velázquez, and Goya, as well as many other masters (such as Rubens, Botticelli, and Caravaggio to name a few). If you only visit one museum in Madrid, this is the one. It’s incredible and worth taking the time to explore. It’s one of the biggest museums in the world, too. Make sure you spend a few hours here at a minimum.

Just a 10-minute walk along the Paseo del Prado, the journey continues at the Thyssen-Bornemisza Museum, a private collection spanning from the Renaissance to Pop Art, and culminates at the Reina Sofía Museum. The Reina Sofía National Art Center offers a fantastic collection of modern art. Works by masters like Picasso, Miró, Kandinsky, Dalí, and Bacon can all be found here. The centerpiece is Picasso’s famous Guernica, a 1937 oil painting considered the most moving anti-war painting in the world. While I don’t love modern art, even I enjoyed this museum.

After museum hopping, it’s time to dive into Madrid’s culinary scene. Try Taberna La Fragua de Vulcano for a rustic atmosphere perfect for sampling cocido madrileño. If you are near the Reina Sofía Museum, don’t miss the vibrant garden terrace at Arzábal, renowned for having some of the best croquetas in the city. Finally, for a unique setting, Bodega de los Secretos lets you dine in restored 17th-century wine caves, making it the most atmospheric choice near the Prado Museum.

According to recent reports, after a late lunch, spend some time exploring Madrid’s unique ‘House Museums. These are former private palaces that preserve the intimate atmosphere of their original owners. The crown jewel of this collection is the Sorolla Museum, the sun-drenched former residence of ‘the painter of light.’ Following a major architectural renovation, this underrated museum is set to reopen its doors in 2026, offering a refreshed look at its stunning gardens and Mediterranean canvases.

Or if you want something else, there is also the nearby Museum of Romanticism, where you can enjoy a coffee in its secret garden, or visit the Lázaro Galdiano Museum to marvel at a private collection of Goya, Murillo, Velázquez, El Greco, or Bosch housed in a magnificent neo-Renaissance mansion.

In the evening, enjoy some food and relaxation.

The second day delves into the medieval and Renaissance layout of the city, famously known as Habsburg Madrid (Madrid de los Austrias). The central hub is Puerta del Sol, where a photo at Kilometer Zero and the Bear and the Strawberry Tree statue are mandatory for a traveler’s geographic check-in. Kilometer Zero is the official starting point of all the highways and railways in the country, making this effectively the center of the entire country. There’s a small plaque you can snap a photo of.

It has been revealed that nearby is the Bear and the Strawberry Tree statue (El Oso y el Madroño). The statue demonstrates a bear reaching up to eat fruit from a madroño tree, symbols which come from Madrid’s coat of arms (the bear represents the city and the tree represents the land and nature surrounding it that has helped make it prosper).

Industry observers note that from here, walk toward the iconic Plaza Mayor, highlighting its porticoed architecture and the Casa de la Panadería. Plaza Mayor once hosted bullfights, markets, symphonies, tournaments, and even executions. Now it’s ringed with tourist shops, cafés, and restaurants. It’s a good place from which to indulge in some people-watching, offers some good (though overpriced) bars, and occasionally has concerts and events.

For a true “Local Life” experience, stop for a calamari sandwich in the nearby alleys. Your taste buds will thank you.

After a relaxing lunch and some people watching, head to the Royal Palace of Madrid. The largest palace in Western Europe, the Baroque-style palace was built in the 18th century and is home to over 3,400 lavishly decorated rooms. It was originally built on a former 9th-century Muslim fort and today functions much like an art museum with numerous works, including pieces by Caravaggio, Juan de Flandes, and Francisco Goya. Though it’s the official residence of the royal family, they don’t actually live here anymore, and the palace is only used for official state functions. You can walk through the palace (both self-guided and guided tours are available), starting at the grand stairway, and wander through lavishly decorated staterooms. There’s also the Royal Armory, which houses a collection of medieval weapons and armor.

To end the day, head to the Almudena Cathedral. Unlike many of the famous medieval churches in Europe, this one was constructed in the late 19th century. It was finally completed in 1993 and was consecrated by Pope John Paul II. While the exterior has a Neo-Classical design (to match the nearby palace), the cathedral also has a Neo-Romanesque crypt with over 400 columns that you can explore. Be sure to head up to the dome for stunning views out over the city.

Madrid is a paradise for foodies. It’s one of the reasons I keep coming back. While there are plenty of food tours to take in Madrid, I suggest heading off on your own to explore. Begin at the city’s iconic gastronomic markets. The glass-walled Mercado de San Miguel is a must for gourmet tapas near Plaza Mayor. It’s popular with the after-work crowd and is a place I usually visit a few times on my trips. Additionally, local favorites like Mercado de San Antón in Chueca and Mercado de Vallehermoso offer a deeper dive into regional flavors. Just make sure to bring an appetite.

If you do want to take a food tour, consider doing a food tour. This post has more of my suggestions.

Sources indicate that for dinner, head to Sobrino de Botín, officially recognized by the Guinness World Records as the world’s oldest restaurant. It was actually a favorite of Ernest Hemingway during his time in Madrid. For a more casual vibe, go ‘tapas crawling’ through the historic streets of La Latina or Barrio de las Letras.

It has been revealed that as the sun sets, head to the Gran Vía to experience Madrid’s world-class rooftop culture. Venues like The Roof at Picalagartos or RIU, 360º sky bar offer signature cocktails and dinner with breathtaking 360-degree views of the skyline.

For those who don’t eat meat, Madrid has actually evolved into one of Europe’s best veg hubs, boasting a vibrant vegetarian and vegan scene in neighborhoods like Malasaña, where plant-based versions of traditional Spanish dishes are now a staple of the city’s diverse culinary identity.

Sources indicate that madrid is the only European capital where nature, science, and royal history converge in a UNESCO World Heritage oasis known as the ‘Paisaje de la Luz‘ (Landscape of Light). But this prestigious area, encompassing the iconic El Retiro Park and the Paseo del Prado, is just the beginning of Spain’s monumental legacy. For more UNESCO wonders, take a day trip out of the city.

Sources indicate that one popular destination worth visiting is the Monastery of San Lorenzo de El Escorial, a sprawling imperial masterpiece recognized by UNESCO for its historical significance. El Escorial is located just one hour from the city by car and was commissioned by Philip II in the 16th century. It’s a massive palatial complex that includes a monastery, library, palace, basilica, and tomb for Spanish monarchs. Yet as massive as it is, it feels more austere than other palatial complexes, likely owing to its granite walls and symmetrical layout.

Industry observers note that another option for a day trip is the Royal Palace and Gardens of Aranjuez, a World Heritage Cultural Landscape that rivals the beauty of Versailles. Located just one hour south of the city, this was originally a hunting lodge, also commissioned in the 16th century by Philip II. It’s a blend of Renaissance and Baroque styles, with lavish rooms filled with tapestries, porcelain, and ornate decorations. There is lots of greenery and gardens here, which is partly why the royal family used this as their spring residence.

Lastly, there’s the historic university city of Alcalá de Henares, the birthplace of Spanish novelist, poet, and playwright Cervantes (he wrote Don Quixote). Just 45 minutes away by car, it also holds its own UNESCO World Heritage status, offering a perfectly preserved look into the Spanish Golden Age (1492–1659).

On your last day, it’s time to get further off the beaten path. Step back into the Golden Age at the Monastery of Las Descalzas Reales and the nearby Royal Monastery of La Encarnación, two hidden palaces that house breathtaking royal art collections behind their cloistered walls.

The Monastery of Las Descalzas Reales is a convent founded in 1559 by Joanna of Austria (sister of Philip II). The name “Descalzas Reales” (which means “Royal Barefoot Ladies”) refers to the Order of Saint Clare nuns who lived here in relative austerity. What makes this monastery unique is that many aristocratic women took refuge here, often bringing their artworks and other valuables. Over the years, this turned the convent into a veritable treasure trove of art.

The Royal Monastery of La Encarnación was founded in 1611 by the wife of Philip III, Margaret of Austria. It was a royal convent, meaning it had the direct support of the monarchy. While the exterior has an austere Baroque style, the interior is quite lavish, with ornate chapels, colorful frescoes, and lots of religious sculptures and paintings. It’s also home to several notable relics, including a vial noted to contain the blood of Saint Januarius. While tours are available, it’s still an active convent so parts are not open to the public (which, honestly, makes it all the more interesting to see).

To end your day with a local touch, head to the vast Casa de Campo park. This is the largest public park in the city, created in 1931. It covers a whopping 17 square kilometers (6.5 square miles) and includes an artificial lake, lots of paths, a zoo, and even an amusement park. Here, you can enjoy a scenic lunch or dinner at one of the lakeside terraces, offering an unrivaled view of the Royal Palace and Almudena Cathedral across the skyline. It’s the perfect place to end your trip.

While Barcelona tends to get more attention, I think Madrid is one of the best cities in Europe. It boasts a mouthwatering culinary scene, a raucous nightlife, and tons of things to see and do — no matter your interest or budget. I’ve been visiting the city for almost two decades and never get tired of the tapas, architecture, and history. The city just packs so much in and there really is something for everyone here. By following the itinerary above, you’ll see all the main sights while also getting off the beaten path in Spain’s historic capital.

Breaking: Florida’s invasive pythons don’t always stay on the ground, and about 1 in 7 adult sightings were up in trees

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (872 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A USGS study found that invasive Burmese pythons in Florida sometimes climb trees, especially in winter, raising concerns for nesting birds.
  • Sources indicate that burmese pythons invading southern Florida are not primarily tree-dwellers, but some of them climb.
  • For 168 juveniles, the share was about 17 percent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A USGS study found that invasive Burmese pythons in Florida sometimes climb trees, especially in winter, raising concerns for nesting birds.

Sources indicate that burmese pythons invading southern Florida are not primarily tree-dwellers, but some of them climb. Among 188 radio-tracked adults, about 14 percent, or roughly 1 in 7, were found in a tree or shrub at least once, according to the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS).

For 168 juveniles, the share was about 17 percent. Across more than 4,000 observations, however, fewer than 3 percent placed a python in a tree or shrub.

Both age groups were most likely to climb in December and January, the cooler months of southern Florida’s dry season.

Each observation came from locating a snake through radio telemetry, not from a chance sighting. Tracking ran from November 2017 to December 2024 in Significant Cypress National Preserve.

Lisa McBride, a biologist at the USGS Fort Collins Science Center, is the study’s first author.

A public USGS data release lists 112 tracking events in trees or shrubs, involving 56 different pythons.

The first python was observed in the Everglades in 1979, but no more were seen until 1995. The species now breeds in the preserve and is spreading through south Florida.

Burmese pythons, one of Florida’s invasive reptiles, are notoriously difficult to find. By some estimates, the probability of detecting an individual python can be less than 5 percent.

Sources indicate that adults in trees were seen basking, resting, brooding eggs or gathering with other pythons. Juveniles rested, basked or moved between tree limbs.

Most adults found in trees during the peak climbing months were basking, a behavior that lets reptiles absorb heat from their surroundings.

The researchers suggest pythons may use trees and shrubs at that time of year to maintain a high body temperature.

In February 2022, one adult male basked atop a Brazilian peppertree about 16 feet (5 meters) above the ground. It then climbed to the crown of a cabbage palm, about 23 feet (7 meters) up.

A female brooded her eggs in a fallen, hollow cypress tree about 6.5 feet (2 meters) above the ground in May 2022.

A juvenile female rested on a pond apple tree about 5 feet (1.5 meters) up that same May.

A USGS video shows a juvenile female moving across the branches of a dahoon holly tree in the preserve.

The higher share among juveniles may reflect an ontogenetic shift, a change in habitat use as an animal grows, the researchers suggest.

The probability of finding a python in a tree generally fell as its weight rose. Smaller snakes may move through branches more easily than heavy adults.

Still, trees with strong branches, such as Brazilian peppertrees and live oaks, supported some of the largest pythons tracked.

Adults caught in Florida average 6 to 9 feet (1.8 to 2.7 meters), according to the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC). The species can reach 19 feet (5.8 meters), however.

Native from India to lower China, the Malay Peninsula and some islands of the East Indies, Burmese pythons are semi-aquatic and excellent climbers.

In a recent development, the exact route of their introduction is unknown. Pythons likely escaped from a breeding facility destroyed during Hurricane Andrew, and pet pythons have likely been released in and around the Everglades.

The months when adult pythons were most likely to be in trees overlap with the nesting season of several wading-bird species. Earlier studies documented pythons preying on nests of great egrets and white ibises in the Everglades.

No python was seen preying on birds in trees during the tracking. The USGS cautioned that the overlap does not mean tree use is causing bird declines.

Rather, it identifies another behavior that could bring an invasive predator into contact with vulnerable animals, and an area for continued research.

More than 25 percent of captured pythons have birds in their stomachs.

Industry observers note that before 2000, mammals were encountered frequently during nocturnal road surveys in Everglades National Park. Road surveys from 2003 to 2011 then recorded a 99.3 percent drop in raccoon observations as pythons spread.

Opossum observations fell by 98.9 percent and bobcat observations by 87.5 percent. The same surveys failed to detect rabbits.

Some reports put the south Florida python population anywhere from 5,000 to 180,000 snakes, though the best estimates so far place it closer to 30,000.

Almost 28,000 wild Burmese pythons have been removed from Florida’s environment and reported to the FWC since 2000. The 2026 Florida Python Challenge alone removed 280, with 907 participants from 30 U.S. states, Canada and Vietnam.

The South Florida Water Management District also pays agents an hourly rate to hunt pythons. They earn $50 for each snake up to 4 feet (1.2 meters), $25 for each additional foot (0.3 meters) and $200 for each verified active nest.

Seasonal data on tree use “could improve the effectiveness of removal efforts by management agencies,” the authors wrote.

Knowing when pythons climb could also help scientists understand how the snakes interact with the Greater Everglades ecosystem.

The study was published in the journal Journal of Herpetology.

Breaking: A dinosaur found by a Montana rancher on her land in 2019 sold for $47.3 million, over five times its top estimate

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (887 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A Nanotyrannus skeleton nicknamed Jodi sold for $47.3 million at Sotheby's in 2026, raising concerns about scientific access to rare fossils.
  • A Nanotyrannus skeleton nicknamed “Jodi” sold at Sotheby’s in Fresh York on October 27, 2026, for a final price of $47.3 million.
  • Jodi Pierson found the skeleton in 2019 on her privately owned land near the town of Jordan, in Garfield County, Montana.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Nanotyrannus skeleton nicknamed Jodi sold for $47.3 million at Sotheby's in 2026, raising concerns about scientific access to rare fossils.

A Nanotyrannus skeleton nicknamed “Jodi” sold at Sotheby’s in Fresh York on October 27, 2026, for a final price of $47.3 million. Its pre-sale estimate was $6 million to $9 million.

Jodi Pierson found the skeleton in 2019 on her privately owned land near the town of Jordan, in Garfield County, Montana.

It has been revealed that six bidders competed for more than 12 minutes, the auction house said. Jodi is now the second most valuable dinosaur ever sold at auction.

The record belongs to “Gus,” a Tyrannosaurus rex skeleton that sold at Sotheby’s Fresh York for $50.1 million on July 14, 2026.

According to Guinness World Records, Gus broke the record set by “Apex,” a Stegosaurus also sold at Sotheby’s New York. Apex fetched $44.6 million on July 17, 2024.

According to recent reports, sotheby’s reports its results including the buyer’s premium, the fee added to the winning bid. The hammer price for Jodi has not been made public.

Jodi was the only lot in its own dedicated sale. Neither the buyer nor the seller has been named.

Its listed provenance is a private collection that acquired the skeleton in 2021.

Industry observers note that sotheby’s lists Jodi as Nanotyrannus cf. lancensis, from the Hell Creek Formation, about 67 million years old. The abbreviation “cf.” marks a provisional identification.

According to recent reports, A crew of seven, including Pierson and Clayton Phipps, dug up the skeleton in a single field season. It comprises about 191 fossil bone elements from one individual.

Recent findings suggest that its virtually complete skull has 53 bones and roughly 50 teeth. The rarely preserved wishbone is intact, and about half of the belly ribs, or gastralia, survived.

According to recent reports, missing parts were restored with 3D-printed and sculpted elements, and the mounted skeleton measures about 19.6 feet (6 meters) from nose to tail. It stands about 9 feet 6 inches (2.9 meters) tall, not 6 feet 5 inches (2 meters) as first listed.

In a recent development, the auction house describes the animal as an adult, based on its overall size and degree of bone development. It cites no peer-reviewed study of the skeleton.

At the Frieze Masters art fair in 2023, the same skeleton was exhibited as a juvenile T. rex.

For decades, many paleontologists argued that Nanotyrannus fossils were simply young T. rex. The debate centered on a skull collected in Montana in 1942 by the Cleveland Museum of Natural History.

In 1988, a team that included museum curator Dr. Michael Williams named it Nanotyrannus lancensis. In December 2025, a study in Science found that the skull’s throat bone had stopped growing, indicating a mature animal.

In October 2025, a study in Nature concluded that the tyrannosaur in the “Dueling Dinosaurs” fossil was a fully grown Nanotyrannus lancensis. Growth rings and fused vertebrae put its age at about 20 years.

Recent findings suggest that that animal had larger forelimbs, more teeth and fewer tail vertebrae than T. rex, the North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences reported.

After examining more than 200 tyrannosaur fossils, the researchers also named a second species, Nanotyrannus lethaeus, after the River Lethe of Greek mythology.

Sources indicate that “This fossil doesn’t just settle the debate. It flips decades of T. rex research on its head,” Lindsay Zanno, head of paleontology at the North Carolina museum and a co-author of the study, stated in 2025.

According to recent reports, before the Gus auction, the Society of Vertebrate Paleontology issued a statement on scientifically significant fossils. It called for them to be permanently curated in accredited museums, universities and other public research institutions.

Without provisions for long-term access, private ownership may permanently diminish opportunities for future research, education and public engagement, the society warned. It also recognized the key role of private landowners, amateur fossil enthusiasts and commercial excavators.

“The discovery of an important fossil is only the beginning of its scientific story,” said Kristina Curry Rogers, the society’s vice president at the time.

Recent findings suggest that “Many of the most significant advances in paleontology have come years or even decades after a fossil was collected,” she noted. Newly introduced analytical methods and technologies allowed scientists to ask entirely new questions of specimens already housed in museums.

After the Jodi sale, Curry Rogers and Zanno published an opinion piece on fossil auctions. They wrote that they hope the fresh owner will make Jodi available for scientific study and public education.

Under Montana law, fossils are part of the surface estate, so they normally belong to whoever owns the land.

The provision, enacted in 2019, says the word “minerals” does not include fossils unless a deed or other instrument clearly states otherwise. A landowner can sever fossil rights from the land through a clear and express grant.

Sotheby’s offered Jodi with full rights and documentation certifying its condition, authenticity and the legality of its ownership.

The federal Paleontological Resources Preservation Act of 2009 does not apply to state, private or Indian lands, according to the Bureau of Land Management.

The information was obtained from Sotheby’s.

Meet the Planimal: Half Hamster Cell, Half Algae, 100% Weird

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, almost all of the major events that changed the trajectory of life on Earth had impossibly tiny beginnings, and the rise of plant life is no exception.
  • Despite the vast evolutionary gulf between them (the two lineages diverged in the middle of the Proterozoic Eon), a upcoming study published in the journal Nature Communications suggests that the cells derived from red algae and mammals still have the capacity to acquire genetic material through a process known as “horizontal gene transfer.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

In a recent development, almost all of the major events that changed the trajectory of life on Earth had impossibly tiny beginnings, and the rise of plant life is no exception. Some 1.5 billion years ago, a eukaryotic cell engulfed a cyanobacterium, which eventually evolved into the chloroplast, the specialized organelle that drives photosynthesis in algae and plants. Other eukaryotic cells, of course, took a very different path, giving rise to all animals and, ultimately, the mammalian cells that make up you and me.

Despite the vast evolutionary gulf between them (the two lineages diverged in the middle of the Proterozoic Eon), a upcoming study published in the journal Nature Communications suggests that the cells derived from red algae and mammals still have the capacity to acquire genetic material through a process known as “horizontal gene transfer.”.

According to recent reports, obviously, most gene transfers in nature move from parents to offspring (fittingly named “vertical gene transfer”), but sometimes cells will acquire traits from other individuals, strains, or even entire species. This is seen most commonly in bacteria that share antibiotic resistance genes, or ARGs, creating troublesome antimicrobial-resistant (or drug-resistant) superbugs in the process. However, other fascinating examples exist, including a parasitic worm that can control its host by swapping genes. In their new study, a team of scientists led by researchers at the University of Tokyo explored whether a similar process could take place between cells separated by more than a billion years of evolution, resulting in what the researchers call “planimal” cells.

“We wanted to understand whether entire chromosomes could cross the enormous evolutionary divide between algae and animals and whether animal cells could stably maintain and pass on such foreign genetic material to their daughter cells,” University of Tokyo biologist Sachihiro Matsunaga, senior author of the study, noted in a press statement. “These questions are fundamental to understanding how genetic material can move across species boundaries and contribute to evolution.”.

Industry observers note that to investigate this possibility, the authors relied on cells derived from the red alga Cyanidioschyzon merolae, along with mammal cells originating from a hamster. Mirroring the primordial event that gave rise to plant life, the researchers allowed the mammalian cell to engulf the alga, after which—surprisingly—cell fusion produced stable hybrid cells. Armed with advanced imaging and genome sequencing, Matsunaga and his team could track how well host mammalian cells retained this algal DNA over subsequent generations. They found that 16.3 million algal base pairs and intact chromosome sequences from all 20 algal chromosomes were retained, and the algal DNA remained detectable through 155 cell generations.

It has been revealed that “Plants and animals cannot reproduce with each other, so their chromosomes are never combined through mating. Yet, we have succeeded in creating hybrid chromosomes containing genetic material from both an alga and a mammal,” Matsunaga mentioned. “This demonstrates that even the vast evolutionary divide between plants and animals can be crossed at the level of chromosomes, without reproduction.”.

The key to the planimal cells’ survival was the epigenetic “gatekeeping” ability of the host cell to essentially silence incorporated foreign DNA. The authors estimate that roughly 96 percent of the algal protein-coding genes were basically offline, but it’s possible that future studies could detect how to flip this gene switch to “on.”.

“Our ultimate goal is to activate these biological pathways and give animal cells some of the unique abilities of plants and algae,” Matsunaga added. “Imagine animal cells that could sustain photosynthesis for long periods, producing oxygen while using carbon dioxide to make useful organic compounds.”.

For 15 years, biologists in a Nevada national park watched nearly all its rattlesnakes return to the same winter den

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (887 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A 15-year study of Great Basin rattlesnakes reveals how they share winter dens, travel miles each spring and return to the same shelters.
  • Great Basin rattlesnakes (Crotalus lutosus) spend the winter together in ancestral dens, then scatter in spring to forage, mate and give birth.
  • “Site fidelity is high at communal dens and nearly all individuals return to their hibernaculum in the fall,” wrote Bryan Hamilton, wildlife biologist at Great Basin National Park in Nevada.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A 15-year study of Great Basin rattlesnakes reveals how they share winter dens, travel miles each spring and return to the same shelters.

Great Basin rattlesnakes (Crotalus lutosus) spend the winter together in ancestral dens, then scatter in spring to forage, mate and give birth.

“Site fidelity is high at communal dens and nearly all individuals return to their hibernaculum in the fall,” wrote Bryan Hamilton, wildlife biologist at Great Basin National Park in Nevada.

A hibernaculum is a winter den.

Recent findings suggest that the captures themselves measured survival, body size and life span. Hamilton and colleagues caught 401 rattlesnakes a total of 799 times.

Of those snakes, 148 were females and 253 were males, which suggests a male-biased sex ratio. The average animal measured about 23 inches (59 centimeters) from snout to vent and weighed about 6.6 ounces (186 grams).

In a recent development, the work relied on capture-mark-recapture, a method that follows known individuals over time. Each snake was restrained in a clear plastic tube during processing.

In a recent development, snakes were marked by clipping belly scales or with passive integrated transponder tags. Each one was then released at its exact site of capture.

Hamilton’s account places the project in the park, but its size data came from four sites in eastern Nevada and western Utah. Related spring surveys visited dens in the same region about ten times a year.

Mean annual survival was estimated at 0.76, or roughly three of every four snakes surviving each year. Average life expectancy was estimated at 3.6 years, with a median of 2.5, though two snakes were recaptured 13 years after first capture.

In 2023, Colton Irons and Kevin Shoemaker of the University of Nevada, Reno tracked those seasonal movements with Hamilton. They captured about 50 of the park’s rattlesnakes from April to October.

In a recent development, the team surgically implanted radio transmitters in 19 of them, 11 males and eight females. Each snake was then located every week to map habitat use before prescribed fires.

“The most adventurous snake we had traveled a total of 4.14 miles to and from their hibernaculum,” the three authors reported.

Recent findings suggest that that distance equals 6.66 kilometers. The route started at 7,311 feet (2,228 meters) and ended at 9,314 feet (2,839 meters) in elevation.

Across 17 years of spring surveys, the mean date of peak captures was April 23, and it moved earlier by about one day per year. Warmer Aprils were associated with earlier emergence from communal rattlesnake dens.

According to recent reports, the number of snakes sharing a winter refuge varies widely among rattlesnakes. Great Basin rattlesnakes “form aggregations of sometimes several hundred individuals for overwintering underground,” states a report on fieldwork at the Idaho National Laboratory site.

Recent findings suggest that in 2019, Matt Goode, an assistant research scientist at the University of Arizona, compared other species. Western diamondbacks often den in groups of up to 10 to 20, he said.

One den of prairie rattlesnakes that he studied in Wyoming held more than 600 snakes. Tiger and black-tailed rattlesnakes, by contrast, tend to den by themselves.

In really cold climates, the ground can freeze up to 4 to 6 feet (1.2 to 1.8 meters) deep. Very large dens probably form there because suitable sites are limited.

It has been revealed that biologists debate whether a reptile’s winter dormancy should be called hibernation or brumation, Goode noted. During it, snakes stop feeding and can remain inactive for a long time.

“Snakes are ectotherms, which means their internal body temperatures do not remain constant like mammals, which are endotherms,” he explained.

Tiger rattlesnakes den in rocky outcrops, in cracks and crevices about 2 to 4 feet (0.6 to 1.2 meters) down.

Recent findings suggest that females come out of the dens earlier than males. Doing so warms their ovaries and lets follicles grow enough to be ovulated.

A 2009 survey of den sites in Arizona, Nevada and Utah, co-authored by Hamilton, compared sunlight at dens with random points in the surrounding habitat.

Its observations suggest that rattlesnakes in cool climates use dens that receive more solar radiation than their surroundings. Dens of Great Basin and black-tailed rattlesnakes fit that pattern, while two western diamondback sites did not.

Industry observers note that implanted data loggers have recorded hourly body temperatures in hibernating timber rattlesnakes in central Tennessee. Over two winters, 53,041 readings averaged 52°F (11.1°C) and ranged from 34°F to 92.7°F (1.1°C to 33.7°C).

Peaks in body temperature marked basking, and 69 percent of those snakes came to the surface two or more times.

Sources indicate that hamilton’s 2018 doctoral dissertation at Brigham Young University modeled the demography of the rattlesnake populations from the long-term dataset. Mean population growth indicated overall stability, though two sites were declining.

Survival contributed overwhelmingly more to population growth than recruitment, the arrival of latest snakes.

In a recent development, rattlesnakes prey mainly on small mammals, so they depend indirectly on snowmelt for survival and reproduction. Declining snowpack is expected to have major impacts on biodiversity.

Among the captured snakes, body condition was weakly correlated with the previous year’s total precipitation.

The information was obtained from the National Park Service.
