Latest Update: Migrating birds may be bringing unusual ticks to Hungary

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (928 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Volunteers in Hungary found 29 Hyalomma ticks over five years, raising the question of whether the ticks are starting to breed there.
  • Hyalomma ticks can carry the virus that causes Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever, a serious and sometimes life-threatening illness.
  • For five years, scientists in Hungary have been asking people to send in any of these ticks they find.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Volunteers in Hungary found 29 Hyalomma ticks over five years, raising the question of whether the ticks are starting to breed there.

Hyalomma ticks can carry the virus that causes Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever, a serious and sometimes life-threatening illness. They usually live in warm, dry places, but lately they keep turning up in Hungary.

For five years, scientists in Hungary have been asking people to send in any of these ticks they find.

What they’ve learned so far raises a simple question: are the ticks just passing through, or are they starting to settle in?

At the HUN-REN Centre for Ecological Research in Budapest, Éva Szabó, Gábor Földvári and their colleagues in the Eco-epidemiology Research Group run the project.

Hyalomma ticks usually live in warm, dry parts of Africa, the Middle East, Asia and southern Europe.

In a recent development, young Hyalomma ticks often feed on birds, including birds that migrate long distances. Adult Hyalomma ticks feed mostly on large animals such as cattle and horses.

The way these ticks feed helps explain how far they can travel. A young Hyalomma tick usually stays on the same animal while it grows.

Recent findings suggest that for Hyalomma marginatum, that’s about three weeks. Ixodes ricinus, the most widespread tick in Hungary, lets go after less than a week each time.

The authors linked the ticks’ spread north to climate change.

The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control keeps a map of where Hyalomma marginatum has turned up in Europe.

Scientists watch these ticks closely because of a virus some of them carry.

The World Health Organization names Hyalomma ticks as the main carrier of Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus. The study’s authors wrote that it’s the most important tick-borne virus affecting people.

According to recent reports, how many people get sick from it each year isn’t clear, because many infections cause no symptoms. The authors cited an estimate of 10,000 to 15,000 cases worldwide.

The World Health Organization estimates that 10% to 40% of reported cases in outbreaks are fatal.

A vaccine has seen limited use in Eastern Europe, and no vaccine is widely available. Treatment relies on supportive care.

Hyalomma ticks hunt their hosts instead of waiting on plants. Dragging a cloth through vegetation, the traditional way to collect ticks, doesn’t work well for them.

So the team relies on citizen scientists instead.

The researchers opened a website called TickWatcher in April 2021.

Four years later, they added a free phone app called PragmaTick. People send in a photo of an odd-looking tick, and an expert checks it.

Industry observers note that by late November 2025, the website had about 107,000 visits. The app had been downloaded 2,500 times. Volunteers had made 1,014 submissions, and 29 turned out to be Hyalomma ticks.

The app won’t accept a report without a date, a place and a photo.

In the app’s first six months, people sent about as many reports through it as they had sent by email in the four and a half years before.

“Successfully involving the public in research can even help unravel problems like finding a needle in a haystack,” the authors wrote.

Thirteen of the 29 ticks were on horses. Five were on buffalo, two on dogs, one on a donkey and one on a cow, and reports came in between mid-June and the end of October.

Horse owners tend to check their animals closely and ride through grass and woods, which may help explain why horses topped the list, the researchers wrote.

News about the program may also have reached some groups of people better than others.

Even so, the authors concluded that owners of livestock and other large animals are likely more affected than other groups.

Three ticks came from people. Four more ticks were crawling with no host, including the one on the kitchen floor.

Industry observers note that most of the 29 were males, 21 in all. One possible reason, according to the authors, is that males may stay on a host longer while they look for mates.

At a buffalo farm near the village of Ágasegyháza, people found four Hyalomma ticks in 2022 and one more in 2023.

Recent findings suggest that two other finds came from within about 9 miles (15 kilometers) of the farm. One was on a cow in 2021, and the other turned up in a garden near the city of Kecskemét in 2023.

All 18 ticks that people mailed in tested negative for the virus. The other 11 were thrown away or destroyed by the people who found them.

Earlier studies in Hungary found antibodies against the virus in 10 of 2,700 people tested between 2008 and 2017, and in 11 of 1,905 cattle and sheep tested in 2017.

Antibodies show past exposure, not a current infection, and these tests may also react to related viruses.

The biggest open question is whether these ticks are only passing through or starting to survive and breed in Hungary.

Answering that will take time. The team plans to keep collecting reports, with close attention to livestock owners and to places where several ticks have already been found.

For now, the people in the best position to help are the ones already checking their horses and cattle.

Every tick they send in indicates scientists a little more about where these ticks are turning up.

The full study was published in the journal Current Research in Parasitology and Vector-Borne Diseases.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, california Rep. Ken Calvert walks down the House steps after votes on Sept. 3. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

Rep. Ken Calvert defeated Rep. Young Kim in a redrawn Southern California district that pitted the two Republicans against one another.

Calvert was leading his rival by 7 points Monday night when The Associated Press called the race for California’s 40th District with more than 70 percent of the vote in.

Calvert, who chairs the powerful House Defense Appropriations Subcommittee, is the longest-serving Republican in the California delegation, first winning election to Congress in 1992.

The race was reshaped by the Golden State’s new voter-approved House map, drawn by state Democrats in response to mid-decade redistricting by Texas Republicans. The new map dismantled Calvert’s 41st District in Riverside County, transforming it into a safely blue Democratic seat in the Los Angeles area. That prompted him to run for the redrawn 40th District, which included a sizable percentage of his current constituents.

Sources indicate that the rare intraparty general election was possible because Calvert and Kim finished in the top two slots in the state’s June primary. Under the California system, all candidates run on the same primary ballot, with the top two vote-getters, regardless of party, advancing to November.

Calvert had already declared victory last week, saying on social media that there was “no greater honor than serving my neighbors and our communities in Congress.”.

Kim’s defeat is the second of her congressional career — she lost her initial bid during the 2018 blue wave before winning election to the House two years later.

According to recent reports, in her concession message, Kim singled out California Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom, who led the redistricting effort last year that targeted five Republican-held districts. Democrats flipped all five seats last week.

“It’s unfortunate that Gavin Newsom’s political redistricting scheme forced two Republican members from Congress into this race,’’ she said in a statement.

Recent findings suggest that the race between was marked by rancor, with Calvert alleging that Kim was not a true conservative and supported higher taxes. Kim accused Calvert of growing rich off stock trades over his decades in Washington.

Calvert will serve in a delegation with a dramatically smaller GOP presence next year, with Democrats likely to hold 48 of California’s 52 House seats. Just two other California Republicans – Reps. Vince Fong and Tom McClintock – have been reelected so far, while a third, Rep. Jay Obernolte, narrowly leads his Democratic challenger in an as-yet-uncalled race.

The Calvert-Kim battle was not the only all-party November clash in California, with several districts featuring matchups between two Democrats.

One incumbent has already been unseated, with Rep. Jimmy Gomez losing to fellow Democrat Angela Gonzales-Torres in the Los Angeles-area 34th District, according to The Associated Press.

Two other blue-on-blue contests in Northern California remained uncalled as of Tuesday afternoon: Rep. Mike Thompson was trailing venture capitalist Eric Jones in the 4th District, while Rep. Doris Matsui led Sacramento City Councilmember Mai Vang in the 7th District.

Industry News: Extreme heat is killing more people, and scientists have estimated how much warming is to blame

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (953 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A Lancet Countdown report found that annual heat-related deaths rose 36% worldwide, with human-caused warming accounting for more than two-thirds of the recent toll.
  • It has been revealed that the Paris Agreement took effect in 2016.
  • That was about 36% higher than the annual average from 2006 through 2015.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Lancet Countdown report found that annual heat-related deaths rose 36% worldwide, with human-caused warming accounting for more than two-thirds of the recent toll.

It has been revealed that the Paris Agreement took effect in 2016. From 2016 through 2023, an estimated 540,800 people died from heat worldwide each year, on average.

That was about 36% higher than the annual average from 2006 through 2015.

The share of heat-related deaths attributed to human-caused warming rose from 55% to 68%.

A project based at University College London, the Lancet Countdown, produced the figures in its tenth annual report, which tracks 54 measures of how climate change affects health.

It was written by 146 researchers and produced with the World Health Organization. Every death count in it is an estimate from models, not a tally of death certificates.

In an interview with Earth.com, Jennifer Israelsson, a senior research fellow at the Lancet Countdown, noted the finding that surprised her most was not a number from the heat data.

It was “the sharp decline in political engagement with the climate-health agenda, despite multiple years with record-breaking temperatures, deadly heatwaves and devastating flooding events across the globe, and the intensification of hurricanes,” Israelsson noted.

Recent findings suggest that between 2006 and 2015, heat was linked to an estimated 398,400 deaths a year. Between 2016 and 2023, it was linked to 540,800 a year, with a range of roughly 369,000 to 681,000.

Sources indicate that near the end of that stretch came the worst year. Heat was linked to a record 710,000 deaths in 2023, and the authors attributed 71.5% of them to human-caused warming.

The researchers attributed an estimated 2.96 million heat-related deaths to human-caused warming from 2016 through 2023.

Annual heat-related deaths attributed to human-caused warming rose by an average of 7,400 per year from 2006 through 2015. From 2016 through 2023, they rose by an average of 15,600 per year.

In a recent development, the researchers used daily temperatures and death records reported at daily, weekly or monthly intervals across 129 countries. They then used models to estimate the global toll.

The second question was how many of those deaths would have occurred in a world with the same weather minus the warming humans have added.

Sources indicate that the authors call the gap between the two the attributable toll. The attribution step is fresh to this year’s report, and the ranges around each figure are wide.

It has been revealed that heat also keeps people from working. The authors estimate 573 billion potential work hours were lost to heat in 2025, 35% above the average for 2006 to 2015.

The lost income came to $1.07 trillion, about 0.9% of global economic output.

The losses were equivalent to 5% of GDP in countries with a low Human Development Index and 0.5% in countries with a very high index.

According to recent reports, the same decade brought real gains. Investment in clean energy reached a record $2.1 trillion in 2025, 82% more than went into fossil fuels.

According to recent reports, the share of electricity from modern renewables rose from 5.5% in 2016 to 13.5% in 2023. Fossil fuels still supplied 80.7% of the world’s energy in 2023.

Where air pollution from fossil fuels fell, the authors counted the benefit. In 75 of 140 countries assessed, cleaner air prevented an estimated 323,000 deaths a year.

Sources indicate that air conditioning tells a mixed story. Its use grew from 32% of households in 2016 to 42% in 2024, and the authors estimate it prevented more than 360,000 heat deaths in each of 2022 and 2023.

In countries with a low Human Development Index, only 3% of households had air conditioning in 2024.

Israelsson told Earth.com the single change that would save the most lives from heat is a heat-health action blueprint.

That means a warning system that reaches hospitals and the public in time, plus measures for cooler buildings and safe working conditions.

She pointed to the Netherlands, which she said has seen heat deaths fall since it adopted a heatwave plan.

Extreme drought covered 51.8% of the world’s land for at least a month in 2025, the second-highest extent on record after 2023.

Since 2016, the area in drought each year has grown about eight times as fast as it did in the previous decade.

Very heavy rainfall affected an average of 17.2% of the world’s land each year from 2016 through 2025, up from 14.8% in the previous decade.

Such downpours can increase the risk of floods, landslides and waterborne disease.

The number of people affected per storm or flood rose more slowly in countries with health early warning systems.

The annual increase was 8.6% smaller than in countries without those systems.

Whether the acceleration continues is the open question, and the authors wrote as much. The heat figures run only through 2023, and the drought and rainfall trends through 2025.

The authors’ answer is to have climate change formally declared a global health emergency.

Israelsson stated the WHO’s existing emergency mechanism was built for short, acute outbreaks like Ebola and “is not designed for long-term emergencies.”.

A new instrument with the same kind of roles and responsibilities, aimed at long-term resilience, is needed, she said.

“A decade after the Paris Agreement, our findings are unambiguous: the health harms of climate change are growing faster than the world’s response to them, and in many cases even accelerating,” noted Marina Romanello, the Lancet Countdown’s executive director.

The report was published ahead of the COP31 climate talks.

The full study was published in the journal The Lancet.

#65734. Breaking: Webb looked at a giant black hole from the dawn of the universe and saw something unexpected beside it

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1133 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Webb looked at a giant black hole from the dawn of the universe and saw something unexpected beside it

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1133 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Webb spotted a faint light beside a giant black hole just 900 million years after the Significant Bang, and astronomers think it may come from a second black hole.
  • It has been revealed that giant black holes from the young universe still puzzle astronomers.
  • The pair, nicknamed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua, dates to just 900 million years after the Massive Bang.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Webb spotted a faint light beside a giant black hole just 900 million years after the Significant Bang, and astronomers think it may come from a second black hole.

It has been revealed that giant black holes from the young universe still puzzle astronomers. Now a team has found what looks like two of them, close together and both feeding.

The pair, nicknamed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua, dates to just 900 million years after the Massive Bang.

If confirmed, it would be the closest-spaced quasar pair known from cosmic dawn.

In a recent development, A quasar is the brilliant glow produced as gas falls toward a supermassive black hole. That glow can outshine all the stars in its galaxy combined.

Silvia Onorato, a postdoctoral research associate at NSF NOIRLab, led the study.

Her team thinks pairs like this one may mark places where young galaxies were crowding together, feeding latest stars and fast-growing black holes at the same time.

It has been revealed that the researchers lean toward two real quasars. They haven’t ruled out, though, that the fainter one is a copy of the brighter one, made when light bends around a galaxy in between.

“There is no definitive theoretical explanation for how a single one of these giant quasars exists so early in the age of our Universe, much less two,” Onorato said.

“We observed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua at a time when the Universe was only a thirteenth of its age and astonishingly, its supermassive black holes are just as massive as those we see today.”.

The universe’s first billion years, a period astronomers call cosmic dawn, were busy.

Clumps of dark matter collapsed, galaxies made their first stars, and the first supermassive black holes took shape at the centers of the biggest galaxies.

Galaxies back then often ran into each other, and some merged completely.

Sources indicate that when galaxies collide, gas can funnel toward their central black holes. The gas heats up as it spirals inward, producing the light we see from a quasar.

Since galaxies collided so often, astronomers expect plenty of quasar pairs closer together than the width of a typical galaxy.

So why have so few turned up? Part of the problem is timing, since a black hole shines as a quasar for only a short part of its life.

Sources indicate that distance is the other problem. Quasars from cosmic dawn are so far away that they look faint and are hard to detect from the ground. And when two of them are very close together, it’s hard to tell one from the other.

Those hurdles make Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua a rare find. If confirmed, it would be the third known quasar pair from cosmic dawn.

Industry observers note that the pair’s Hawaiian name was created through the A Hua He Inoa program at the ʻImiloa Astronomy Center of Hawaiʻi. The University of Hawaiʻi’s Hawaiian Language College, Ka Haka ʻUla O Keʻelikōlani, also took part.

In English, the name means “Two celestial bodies of fathomless powerful darkness in the brilliance of heat reincarnating energy into the Universe.”.

Astronomers found the pair in the Aether survey, a James Webb Space Telescope program that’s taking a census of objects in the early universe.

Emanuele Paolo Farina, an associate scientist at NSF NOIRLab/Gemini, leads the survey.

According to recent reports, farina’s team used Webb to split the light of 200 quasars into its colors, point by point. That’s 43% of all the quasars known from this stage of cosmic history.

Recent findings suggest that onorato’s team checked every one by eye. Next to J1602+4228A, a quasar first reported in 2004, they spotted a second, fainter source. No other quasar in the survey had a companion like it.

The faint one, J1602+4228B, is so dim and so close to its partner that seeing it from the ground should have been nearly impossible.

Earlier Gemini observations from a 2017 program had pointed only at the brighter quasar.

The team went back with Gemini North, a telescope on Maunakea, a dormant volcano in Hawaiʻi, and recorded each quasar’s light separately.

“The sky over Maunakea was so clean and sharp that we managed to collect the data in only two nights,” Onorato remarked.

The brighter quasar’s black hole weighs about 1.5 billion times as much as the Sun. Its partner’s comes in at about 400 million, roughly a quarter as heavy.

As seen from Earth, the two are about 18,100 light-years apart, or about one-fifth the width of the Milky Way.

The two quasars’ light was stretched by almost exactly the same amount on its way here, which means they’re at nearly the same distance from us.

Both black holes are pulling in matter near or slightly above the Eddington limit. At that point, light from the falling gas pushes outward about as hard as gravity pulls inward.

Feeding that fast is typical for quasars this early, the researchers wrote.

The fainter quasar also looks redder, a sign that more dust is blocking its light.

Industry observers note that could the second quasar be a copy of the first? A massive galaxy between Earth and a quasar can bend the quasar’s light and make two or more copies of it. Astronomers call this gravitational lensing.

To test the idea, the team looked at light from gas spread across hundreds of light-years around each black hole.

Stars inside a lensing galaxy can distort light from a small area near a black hole, but not from gas spread that widely.

Sources indicate that the light from the gas demonstrated different patterns in the two spectra. The brighter source showed a stronger signature of gas flowing outward.

The researchers wrote that this difference favors two separate quasars.

Older Hubble images do show a galaxy near the line of sight to the fainter quasar, which could hold the extra dust or act as a lens. Its spread-out look suggests it’s fairly close to us, making strong lensing unlikely.

Even so, the team wrote, spectra alone can’t definitively rule out lensing.

Based on how quasars cluster over larger distances, a pair this close should be extremely rare.

Recent findings suggest that yet one turned up among the 199 quasars the team searched around. That’s roughly 100 to 1,000 times more clustering than the predictions suggest.

Predictions at such small distances are very uncertain, though, and one pair can’t show whether close pairs are really this common.

“Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua is a really unique environment,” Onorato said.

“It’s a laboratory for astronomers to study how the very first massive galaxies and their central black holes assembled together through direct galaxy interactions during these early times.”.

The full study was published in the journal The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

A brain region known for listening helps us speak

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • WASHINGTON — A part of the brain famous for listening is notable for talking, too.
  • Data collected from people as they listen and try to talk show that this brain region, a small spot inside a larger area called Wernicke’s area, has a more expansive job than researchers thought when it comes to communicating.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

WASHINGTON — A part of the brain famous for listening is notable for talking, too.

Data collected from people as they listen and try to talk show that this brain region, a small spot inside a larger area called Wernicke’s area, has a more expansive job than researchers thought when it comes to communicating. The results may help efforts to restore people’s voices. The results presented November 15 at the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience and published November 19 in Science.The study provides convincing evidence that this brain spot is critical for speech production, says neurologist and language researcher Jeffrey Binder of the Medical College of Wisconsin in Milwaukee. “My hope is that this study will help scientists and clinicians accept a more accurate interpretation of this focal area” as an early stop on the pathway to saying a word.

A small part of the brain, just above the left ear, was first described in 1874 by a neurologist Carl Wernicke as necessary for making sense of speech. People with damage there had trouble comprehending words. But some people also had trouble producing them. “Sounds were swapped, words were replaced with near misses,” Edward Chang of the University of California, San Francisco, said in a news briefing. “The basic question has been, ‘Why would damage to a hearing area of the brain break the ability to speak?’ That question has been open for 150 years.”The new research offers an answer: A small bit of Wernicke’s area (to be extremely specific, the left posterior superior temporal gyrus or lpSTG ) becomes active just before a word is spoken. “Every word that you have said today began in that small part above your left ear about a quarter of a second before you said it,” Chang said.

Industry observers note that the finding adds to growing evidence that brain areas are more complex than people have appreciated, states neuroscientist Leigh Hochberg at Brown University in Providence, R.I. “I believe that one of the things we are going to learn over the next five, 10 years of this research, is that each part of the brain that, we were taught as a med student or a grad student, does this, probably does that and a whole lot more.”.

Scientists measured brain activity in 28 people before they had surgery for epilepsy or tumors. They were able to see that this brain region kicked on as a person listened to words, and also just before they attempted to speak. Cells there had preferences for certain sorts of words, long ones, for instance. “It’s more active when you’re about to say the word caterpillar than when you’re about to say the word cat,” said Matthew Leonard, a cognitive neuroscientist at UCSF.

Electrical stimulation to this small bit of brain also interfered with people’s ability to talk. “What we found was that stimulation, really only in this lpSTG area, disrupted this speech production when it was delivered just prior to speaking,” mentioned UCSF bioengineer Alexander Silva.

According to recent reports, some efforts to make implanted devices that can help restore speech to people who no longer talk focus on the motor cortex, a part of the brain that controls the movements required for speech. This bit of Wernicke’s area offers an additional spot to consider, Silva remarked. “What if you could target a single brain region and gain access to the full spectrum of speech, from listening all the way up to speech production?”.

Experimental brain implants in two volunteers with paralysis were able to detect both what they heard and what they were trying to say, the researchers report in the study.

The discovery may help scientists better understand situations that involve both hearing and speaking, such as speech or comprehension differences in people with autism, or how children first begin learning to talk, Chang stated.

#65731. The future of Caribbean coral reefs may be hidden in their past

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1423 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

The future of Caribbean coral reefs may be hidden in their past

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1423 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ancient coral fossils reveal more possible Caribbean reef habitat by 2100, but warming still threatens every species studied.
  • Recent findings suggest that predictions of coral survival in a warming Caribbean have generally been based on present-day reef records.
  • In a fresh study, mid-Holocene coral fossils dated to 5,000 to 7,000 years ago were incorporated into habitat forecasts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ancient coral fossils reveal more possible Caribbean reef habitat by 2100, but warming still threatens every species studied.

Recent findings suggest that predictions of coral survival in a warming Caribbean have generally been based on present-day reef records. Evidence from fossil reefs now suggests this basis has been too narrow.

In a fresh study, mid-Holocene coral fossils dated to 5,000 to 7,000 years ago were incorporated into habitat forecasts.

Four reef-building species were examined: elkhorn, staghorn, boulder brain and mustard hill corals.

More potential habitat for 2100 was identified once the fossil records had been included in the models.

It has been revealed that the overall decline was not reversed by this additional habitat. Losses of 45% to 100% of suitable habitat were still projected for each species by 2100.

The extent of loss varied by species and by the level of future carbon emissions.

The research was led by Claire Williams at the University of Texas at Austin’s Jackson School of Geosciences.

Two variables were used to build the computer models: sea surface temperature and sea surface salinity.

Water suitability for each coral was estimated by these models. Actual reef growth at any given site was not predicted by them.

In habitat modeling, every recorded location of a species is paired with the water conditions measured there.

Maps of the future ocean are then searched for matching conditions.

Two limitations of models trained on present-day records alone were described by the authors.

It has been revealed that only water conditions found on Earth today can be learned by such models. Locations where a species is right now absent for other reasons are also missed.

Records from a different ocean are supplied by fossils. Caribbean corals have persisted through hundreds of thousands of years of changing conditions.

The fossil period selected here is regarded by researchers as an analog for present-day warming.

Coral occurrence records were obtained from public sources including the Paleobiology Database. Published reef surveys provided further fossil records.

Field observations collected in Jamaica between 2017 and 2024 were added by Williams’s team. At least 16 records per period were available for every species.

Fossil data are useful only if a species’ environmental tolerances have remained stable through time.

A closer match between past and present conditions than chance would produce was found for three species.

Recent findings suggest that elkhorn coral did not reach this statistical threshold. A large overlap between its past and present conditions was still seen.

Extra future habitat was picked up by the fossil-trained models for each of the four species.

Recent findings suggest that as much as 44,200 square miles (114,559 square kilometers) of added habitat was projected for 2100. That is close to the size of Ohio.

No suitable habitat in 2100 was left for elkhorn or mustard hill coral by the modern-only models under high emissions.

Some habitat for both was kept once the fossil data were added. The authors flagged these estimates as highly uncertain.

The two sets of models were framed by the authors as the edges of a likely range.

Under high emissions, models based only on modern records found no suitable habitat for elkhorn or mustard hill coral in the study area by 2100.

Adding fossils revealed some potential habitat for both, though those estimates are highly uncertain.

Heat-stressed corals lose their color in a process called bleaching. Many of them die afterward.

The worst bleaching ever seen in the Northern Hemisphere came after record marine heatwaves in 2023.

Two emissions pathways were tested for each coral. Emissions level off near mid-century in one and keep climbing to 2100 in the other.

Sources indicate that habitat was lost by every species on both pathways. The losses grew under high emissions and from 2050 to 2100.

Industry observers note that boulder brain coral is a massive species that can live for a long time. Its losses were the steepest of all four.

It has been revealed that no suitable habitat was left for it by 2100 under high emissions. Elkhorn coral was left with very little.

This clashes with the official threat status that boulder brain coral presently holds.

The species is ranked as vulnerable by the IUCN, the body that tracks extinction risk worldwide.

Elkhorn and staghorn corals sit one level higher as critically endangered species. Boulder brain coral may be more threatened than once believed, the authors wrote.

The largest share of habitat in 2100 was kept by mustard hill coral on both pathways. It is known as a weedy coral. It spreads easily but builds little reef structure.

Reefs made up mostly of this coral are expected to give less shelter to the sea life people rely on.

The models projected the heaviest habitat losses in the southern Caribbean.

All four species had lost their habitat near 10 degrees north by 2100 under high emissions.

In a recent development, A small patch near 15 degrees north was held only by staghorn coral. Most leftover habitat sat close to 20 degrees north.

The Florida Keys, Cuba and the north coast of Mexico’s Yucatán Peninsula still held habitat.

Sources indicate that no real northward shift of the corals was detected. The southern habitat is simply lost and not moved.

Getting to the habitat that is left poses another problem for the corals.

Linked communities of mustard hill coral have been recorded more than 1,000 miles (1,700 kilometers) apart.

Elkhorn coral has been documented spreading only about 0.6 miles (1 kilometer).

Today, about 33% to 38% of modeled suitable habitat overlaps existing marine protected areas.

By 2100 under high emissions, the models projected that share would fall for mustard hill and elkhorn corals and rise for staghorn coral.

The models found no suitable habitat for boulder brain coral anywhere in the study area under that scenario.

Newly introduced protected areas in the northern Caribbean were called for by the authors.

Closer ties between existing reserves were also urged. Mexico’s Sian Ka’an and the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary were named as examples.

Reef-dependent regions such as Jamaica and the Lesser Antilles are likely to lose all suitable habitat for the four corals studied by 2100.

Industry observers note that rowan Martindale is a co-author and associate professor at the Jackson School. According to her, those places cannot simply be abandoned.

Local communities rely on reefs for fish and for protection from hurricanes, she added.

What Jamaica has already lost was examined in a second study by Williams and colleagues.

Fossil and living reefs in northeast Jamaica were compared in the companion study.

These fossil reefs formed 125,000 to 130,000 years ago and are now exposed above sea level.

The surveys were therefore carried out on foot. Corals were photographed at intervals along measured transect lines.

Staghorn coral made up roughly half of the fossil coral on the seaward reefs at Navy Island and Dragon Point.

Elkhorn coral accounted for about 40% of the fossil community at Dragon Point and about 10% at Navy Island.

According to recent reports, on nearby living reefs, the largely dead branching corals are now covered by algae. Mustard hill coral dominates the surviving coral cover.

Only sea surface temperature and salinity were included in the models. Conditions on the seafloor where corals grow may differ substantially.

Nutrient pollution, turbidity and ocean acidification were not considered in this analysis.

Sources indicate that coral disease and the decline of herbivorous reef animals were also excluded. Further habitat loss from these stresses was anticipated by the authors.

Future water conditions in the Florida Keys and along Cuba’s southern coast will be unlike any fossil or modern record.

Recent findings suggest that those areas are rated suitable by the models, yet corals may be unable to survive there. Future habitat is therefore likely overestimated.

In a recent development, newer climate projections became available only after the analysis had been completed. A warmer and more saline Caribbean is indicated by them.

Smaller changes are projected for the Yucatán, which may allow suitable habitat to persist there longer.

“Conservation needs to be adaptive and to keep learning newly introduced information,” Williams said.

Recent findings suggest that fossils from older warm periods could also be incorporated, according to the authors. Unmatched future conditions would then be reduced.

Future research could also apply this method to reefs in the Indian and Pacific oceans.

The full study was published in the journal Conservation Biology.

Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, center, arrives for a House Republican leadership candidate forum for the 120th Congress in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday, with Rep. Celeste Maloy, R-Utah, walking alongside him. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

House Republicans on Tuesday opted for a newly introduced face atop their ranks, electing Rep. Jim Jordan as the incoming minority leader for the 120th Congress after Republicans suffered massive losses in last week’s midterm elections.

The Ohio Republican defeated outgoing Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., in a closed-door, secret-ballot election. The final tally was 106-73.

In a recent development, “Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families. Democrats offer more government. We will offer more freedom,” Jordan said after the hourslong process.

In a recent development, the two had been working the phones before making their pitches during a candidates forum in the Capitol Visitor Center’s auditorium on Tuesday morning. Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., announced last week he would not seek a leadership post in the newly introduced Congress, which will be seated on Jan. 3.

“Obviously Jim and I know each other, but I’ve got a proven record of how to bring people together,” Scalise noted ahead of the vote, trying to play up his experience, including more than a decade on the leadership team that included a stint as whip.

As House Republicans trickled out of the candidates’ forum for breaks or to take phone calls, one member, granted anonymity to discuss a private session, said Scalise and Jordan “both have strong points, but they both have flaws.” Each made an unsuccessful bid for speaker in 2023 after the ouster of Kevin McCarthy, before the gavel ultimately went to Johnson.

Declining to reveal which would get his vote, the member remarked: “I won’t talk about a secret vote, but I know who I think is best to lead us.”.

The incoming minority conference also selected other leaders on Tuesday.

Majority Whip Tom Emmer of Minnesota held off a challenge from Texas Rep. August Pfluger to become minority whip in January, despite some grumbling about how tight votes were handled on the floor this year.

“We’ve got to retool our whip operation,” Texas Rep. Nathaniel Moran said Tuesday morning, pointing to “the number of times we were held up by either discharge petitions or failed rule votes.”.

“Those were things that should not have happened in the majority,” said Moran as he publicly backed Pfluger for whip.

But Emmer projected confidence after his whip win, comparing the moment to when Republicans were down and out after their losses in 2018 only to rebound a few years later.

It has been revealed that “To our colleagues on the left, enjoy this honeymoon phase, because come Jan. 3, 2027, you will regret ever putting your name on a ballot,” he stated at a news conference, adding that Republicans under his watch would expose the “empty promises” that Democrats made to voters and push back on what he called their “radical” agenda.

Recent findings suggest that in the day’s only three-way race, conference Chair Lisa McClain of Michigan defeated Reps. Erin Houchin of Indiana and Greg Steube of Florida to keep her spot.

“We had a spirited leadership election. There were notable conversations about the future of our conference, and I listened,” McClain said at the news conference.

It has been revealed that in the race to lead House Republicans’ campaign arm, Rep. Brian Jack of Georgia defeated Rep. Rudy Yakym of Indiana, seen as an up-and-coming Ways and Means Committee member. That means Jack will take on a huge share of the uphill task of selecting candidates and raising funds for the 2028 cycle as he helms the National Republican Congressional Committee.

But most of the attention heading into Tuesday’s closed-door proceedings was on the minority leader race.

It has been revealed that johnson, the outgoing speaker, declined to endorse a candidate but had encouraging words for Jordan after his win. “He’s going to do an excellent job. He’s a good, trusted friend and brother,” he said.

According to recent reports, rep. Tom Cole, R-Okla., stated it was a “tough choice for the conference to make,” but he wasn’t disappointed in the pick. “He was an exceptionally capable chairman of both Oversight and Judiciary. He’s excellent in an interview,” Cole said of Jordan. “He’s got boundless energy and determination.”.

Jordan’s victory means he will form a political and legal tag team with newly installed White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller in pushing back on a number of investigations House Democrats have planned for President Donald Trump, some of his second-term administration officials and his business-minded family members.

Democrats will have more than 250 seats in the chamber, with a number of races still uncalled. Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, expected to become the next House speaker, told reporters last week he predicts Democrats will have at least 255 seats when all the ballots have been counted and verification processes have played out.

“It’s a historic majority in the 21st century,” Jeffries told reporters in Washington, D.C., the day after the midterms. “The American people have chosen the economy over extremism. The American people have chosen hope over hatred. The American people have chosen common sense over corruption, chaos and cruelty. The American people have chosen House Democrats because they want to see a dramatic change in direction.”.

Political analysts have predicted an internal battle within the GOP for the direction the party takes over the next two years — and after Trump leaves office in January 2029.

Industry observers note that the Institute for Legislative Analysis, a nonprofit organization that advocates to shrink the size and influence of the government, released a vote study assessment on Monday. Its calculations led ILA to endorse Emmer and three fresh faces: Jordan, Steube and Jack.

“It’s clear many Republican voters feel their representatives in Washington aren’t representing them,” Ryan McGowan, the institute’s CEO, said in a statement. “It will be interesting to see whether House Republicans respond by choosing leaders … whose voting records are much more closely aligned with the party’s conservative base.”.

Several GOP sources late last week, granted anonymity to be candid, mentioned they were expecting a close outcome between Scalise and Jordan, adding Emmer was working the phones hard to remain whip. One said having either Scalise or Jordan atop the conference, with the expectation of Emmer staying on as whip, “won’t be much of a change at the top.”.

The latest leadership team will take over Jan. 3, when Democrats are expected to, in part, use their large majority to target all things Trump 2.0. The same GOP source said the majority party will “inevitably be pursuing impeachment by August recess despite their disciplined statements to the media pre-election.”.

Trump replied in the affirmative when a “60 Minutes” correspondent asked him in an interview that aired Sunday night if he could work with Democrats, should they also be aggressively investigating his team.

In a recent development, “Well, I did it for four years,” the president mentioned of his first term. “They impeached me twice. And there are those that say that worked out to my advantage.”.

Nina Heller, Michael Macagnone and Samantha Freeman contributed to this report.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hubble’s edge-on view of spiral galaxy NGC 1827 reveals dark dust lanes, a bright central bulge and blue patches where stars may be forming.
  • Today’s Image of the Day from Hubble shows a ribbon of rust-colored dust cutting through a bright band of starlight.
  • The ribbon breaks into dark patches toward the edges, and it takes a moment to recognize what you’re looking at: a spiral galaxy seen from the side.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hubble’s edge-on view of spiral galaxy NGC 1827 reveals dark dust lanes, a bright central bulge and blue patches where stars may be forming.

Today’s Image of the Day from Hubble shows a ribbon of rust-colored dust cutting through a bright band of starlight.

The ribbon breaks into dark patches toward the edges, and it takes a moment to recognize what you’re looking at: a spiral galaxy seen from the side.

According to recent reports, the galaxy is NGC 1827. From this angle, the arms that would sweep around its center in a face-on view overlap along our line of sight.

What stands out instead is the structure of the disk itself, from its glowing central bulge to the uneven ribbon of dust that runs through it.

NGC 1827 lies about 37 million light-years away in the constellation Columba, also known as the Dove.

Hubble captured this view with its Advanced Camera for Surveys, and NASA released the image on October 16.

Recent findings suggest that A spiral galaxy’s disk is wide and relatively thin. Its arms curve through that disk, carrying stars, gas and dust.

When we see the disk nearly edge-on, much of that material appears in a narrow strip.

The central bulge, which extends above and below the disk, gives the galaxy its thicker middle.

That geometry also makes the dust especially easy to see. Along parts of the disk, we look through enough dust to dim the combined light of the stars behind it.

The resulting dark lane runs in front of the bright bulge, where the difference between the obscured and unobscured regions is easiest to make out.

Follow the dust lane away from the center and you’ll see bright blue patches scattered across the disk. NASA identifies them as places where newly introduced stars are likely forming.

Hot, massive young stars give off intense blue light. They burn through their fuel rapidly by stellar standards, so a concentration of them can point to relatively recent star formation.

In NGC 1827, those blue patches sit among dark clouds, where gas and dust provide the raw material for future generations of stars.

The side view makes it difficult to tell which arm a particular patch belongs to.

A knot of blue light that appears close to the center in the image could sit farther out in the disk, somewhere along the same line of sight.

Hubble highlights where each feature appears in the image, but its true distance from the galaxy’s center is harder to pin down.

Just left of the galaxy’s bright middle, a star stands out with four sharp spikes.

According to recent reports, it looks close enough to belong to NGC 1827, but it lies between Earth and the galaxy. Its apparent position is a chance alignment.

Those four spikes offer a clue to another kind of structure, this time inside the telescope. They appear when light from a bright point source bends around the supports that hold Hubble’s secondary mirror in place.

The pattern is especially obvious on this star because so much of its light comes from one tiny point in the image.

Industry observers note that other objects sit much farther away. Look into the dark sky beyond the disk and you’ll find small, faint smudges, some of them distant galaxies.

A single frame brings together a foreground star, a nearby spiral and galaxies deeper in the background.

The portrait came from a Hubble program targeting 260 satellite galaxies around 22 hosts similar to the Milky Way.

These smaller galaxies give astronomers a way to test how well models of the universe describe what happens on the scale of individual galaxies and their neighbors.

Computer models can reproduce many of the broad patterns astronomers see across the universe.

The details get harder to match on smaller scales, where the growth of galaxies depends in part on how gas gathers and how stars affect the material around them.

Looking at many satellite systems gives researchers a broader sample for those comparisons.

Hubble’s sharp view is useful because a galaxy’s overall brightness tells only part of its story.

In this image, the narrow dust lane, bright central bulge and scattered blue patches each give a different view of how its material is arranged.

From another vantage point, the spiral arms might be the first thing we’d notice.

From Earth, the most striking feature is the dark streak down the middle, visible because the galaxy’s own stars light it from behind.

Breaking: Solo meerkats can find their way back home

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • It was a hot, dry day in the Kalahari Desert, and Mathilde Martin was running after a meerkat.
  • The animal wore a GPS tracker around its neck and bolted between shelters, like an action hero running for cover, says Martin, a biologist at the University of Zurich.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

It was a hot, dry day in the Kalahari Desert, and Mathilde Martin was running after a meerkat.

The animal wore a GPS tracker around its neck and bolted between shelters, like an action hero running for cover, says Martin, a biologist at the University of Zurich. She and her colleagues had captured the meerkat earlier that morning, driven it 1.5 kilometers from its pack and then released it into the desert. They were trying to find out how well individual meerkats could find their way back home.

It has been revealed that the answer was quite well, the researchers reported November 19 in the Journal of Experimental Biology. The results suggest that meerkats can navigate expertly on their own, perhaps relying on mental maps charted early in life. “They all seem to be very, very good,” Martin says. It’s a surprise finding for a species known for its group cooperation.

In a recent development, meerkats (Suricata suricatta), which live in southern Africa, form tight-knit family groups of up to 50 members. These social animals cooperate in many aspects of life, including by babysitting each other’s pups and watching for predators while traveling along foraging paths. Martin and her colleagues thought meerkats might also rely on one another for navigating. Some pack members, perhaps those who’ve had more opportunity to explore solo, might have spatial knowledge of their territory and lead the rest, she notes. But that’s not what the team discovered.

Recent findings suggest that in separate catch and release experiments with 20 individual meerkats, 18 made a beeline back home, back to their group or back to the site where they were captured. (The other two may have been too stressed to get moving, Martin indicates.).

Recent findings suggest that neither age nor individual experience, which researchers had been tracking, seemed to factor into the meerkats’ homing skills. Nearly all of them knew where to go, Martin says. She thinks these crackerjack navigators relied on visual cues to orient themselves. They’d pop up on their hind legs and scan the landscape before scampering off in a direct line to their target.

It’s likely that scent played a role, too, though distant scent marks may have faded by the time the meerkats were released. The researchers dropped the animals off in territory they hadn’t visited for at least 30 days. “Otherwise,” she says, “it would have been a bit too easy for them to find their way back,” she says.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Adults with cannabis use disorder reported suicidal thoughts far more often than other adults, and the gap held steady for a decade.
  • Adults with cannabis use disorder had 57% higher odds of reporting serious suicidal thoughts in the past year than adults without the disorder, even after researchers accounted for depression and other factors.
  • Industry observers note that across U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Adults with cannabis use disorder reported suicidal thoughts far more often than other adults, and the gap held steady for a decade.

Adults with cannabis use disorder had 57% higher odds of reporting serious suicidal thoughts in the past year than adults without the disorder, even after researchers accounted for depression and other factors.

Industry observers note that across U.S. surveys from 2014 through 2023, researchers found no clear evidence that the link grew stronger.

Industry observers note that cannabis use disorder is not the same as using cannabis. It means having trouble controlling the habit even when it is clearly causing harm.

The survey measured it with nine yes-or-no questions about the past year.

Tosin Philip Oyetunji, a doctoral student in public health at the University of California, Merced, led the study with three colleagues there.

Sources indicate that the team pooled ten years of the National Survey on Drug Use and Health, which the federal government runs every year. After minors and incomplete answers were set aside, 415,861 adults were left.

Among them, 4.0% met the criteria for the disorder. And 4.6% said that in the past 12 months they had seriously thought about killing themselves.

“What we would most like people to understand is that struggling with cannabis use can go hand in hand with mental health challenges that are not always visible,” Oyetunji noted in an interview with Earth.com.

Industry observers note that adults with the disorder had 1.57 times the odds of reporting suicidal thoughts. The range around that figure runs from 1.44 to 1.72.

In a recent development, the comparison is adjusted, which matters more than usual here. The model accounted for depression, serious psychological distress and heavier drinking that met the criteria for alcohol use disorder.

The team also controlled for income, education, insurance, self-rated health, religious attendance and whether a person’s state had legalized recreational cannabis.

In a recent development, so the gap isn’t just depression showing up in a different column. Nobody was followed over time, though, so the survey can’t say which came first.

Recent findings suggest that the team expected the link to strengthen. Cannabis potency has risen sharply since legalization began, and Canadian data had suggested a tightening link.

An earlier national study had also tied cannabis use to suicidal thoughts, plans and attempts.

In a recent development, the researchers found no clear evidence that the link strengthened. In the 2016 and 2022 surveys, the odds ran higher than in the first survey year.

It has been revealed that neither of those two survived the correction the team applied for testing ten years at once. Across the decade, the differences from one survey to the next were too small to rule out chance.

“A public health concern does not have to be getting worse to deserve attention,” Oyetunji stated when Earth.com asked why the link had held while the drug changed.

Sidra Goldman-Mellor, a professor of public health at UC Merced and the study’s senior author, put the other half of it plainly.

“People with cannabis use disorder are still at a very substantially increased likelihood of experiencing serious suicidal thoughts, and that’s not something that is widely understood,” she said.

The disorder was not the only measure that showed the pattern. The survey’s criteria changed partway through the decade, so the team ran the analysis again using how often people used cannabis.

In a recent development, nondaily users had 1.39 times the odds of reporting suicidal thoughts, compared with people who had not used cannabis at all. Daily or near-daily users had 1.65 times the odds.

“This suggests that patterns of cannabis use may also be important to consider when examining mental health, and it raises questions about how the frequency of use relates to suicidal thoughts,” Oyetunji told Earth.com.

The team also split the sample by sex, by age and by race and ethnicity.

Adults with the disorder had higher odds in every one of those groups, and the differences between the groups were too small to call real.

Everyone answered once, so nobody can say which came first. Every answer was also the person’s own account of a year they were remembering.

Recent findings suggest that the study focused on serious suicidal thoughts. The link with cannabis use disorder may differ for suicide plans, attempts or deaths.

The survey also records nothing about what people were using. Potency, product type and whether someone vaped concentrates are all missing, so the study cannot test the potency question it raises.

It has been revealed that studies of high-THC products disagree anyway. A recent review found strong links between high-THC cannabis and the disorder itself or psychosis, and weaker ones for depression and anxiety.

Craving and withdrawal were left out of the disorder measure so the questions would match across years, which probably undercounts it.

The survey excluded people living in institutions and people experiencing homelessness who were outside shelters.

In a recent development, the authors raise one more possibility. As cannabis use spread, the group meeting the criteria may have shifted toward milder cases.

A shift like that would hold the average down even if nothing had changed for the most severe cases.

Two people can give this survey the same answers. In one of them, cannabis use deepened a crisis. In the other, a crisis drove heavier use.

It has been revealed that A single round of questions cannot tell them apart. Researchers would have to follow the same people for years, with the potency and the products written down.

Oyetunji is widening the question rather than narrowing it.

“I want to better understand how these risks overlap, what drives them, and where we may be missing opportunities to help people before they experience serious harm,” he stated.

Clinics don’t have to wait for that. Someone asking for help with cannabis may be carrying something they have not mentioned, and the authors argue that the right response is to ask.

The full study was published in the journal Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs.

It has been revealed that florida Rep. Darren Soto, here at a hearing in July, has won a sixth term representing the 9th District. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

Florida Rep. Darren Soto, the most vulnerable House Democrat running for reelection, narrowly won a sixth term Tuesday in a district that state Republicans redrew in their favor.

Sources indicate that soto was leading Republican Navy veteran Dan Green by less than a point when The Associated Press called the race for Central Florida’s 9th District a week after Election Day. His margin of victory was above the 0.5 percent threshold that would trigger a recount under state law.

House Democrats have so far flipped more than 40 seats and appear on track to hold their biggest majority in the chamber in decades. Soto’s win means that no House Democratic incumbent lost to a Republican in the general election this year. And Florida Democrats defended all four seats the GOP had hoped to pick up under the state’s new Republican-drawn map.

In a recent development, democratic Reps. Kathy Castor and Jared Moskowitz both won reelection from districts that shifted red, while Democrat Pia Dandiya, a former high school principal, defeated Republican Marine Corps veteran Casey Askar for a redrawn open seat in South Florida.

According to recent reports, soto, who declared victory last week, had been seen as the most vulnerable of the targeted Florida Democrats. The upcoming map reduced the Hispanic population of his district as the seat shifted from one that Kamala Harris would have carried in 2024 to one that Donald Trump would have taken by 18 points.

According to recent reports, “Despite the Florida Republican legislature’s efforts to redraw me out of this district, my record of delivering for Florida demonstrated voters that I am a reliable fighter for them in Congress,” Soto remarked in a Nov. 4 statement.

In a Tuesday memo detailing how House Democrats secured their historic majority, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee took aim at Republicans’ mid-decade redistricting efforts, saying their “attempts to steal seats … supremely backfired.”.

While Florida Republicans were unsuccessful in flipping the four Democrat-held seats, the party held all of its House seats in the Sunshine State. Republican Rep. María Elvira Salazar narrowly won reelection in the Miami-area 27th District over Democratic challenger Eliott Rodriguez, the AP reported Tuesday. In the 7th District outside Orlando, Republican former TV news anchor Ryan Elijah defeated Democratic Navy veteran Bale Dalton, a former NASA chief of staff who conceded Tuesday.

A fast-growing heart is good for the Grinch. People are another story

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (960 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • It has been revealed that in the classic Dr.
  • Industry observers note that “They say that the Grinch’s small heart grew three sizes that day,” giving him “the strength of 10 Grinches plus two,” says the narrator of the 1966 movie version.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

It has been revealed that in the classic Dr. Seuss tale, How the Grinch Stole Christmas, the Grinch starts out with a heart “two sizes too small.” He’s a mean one, disguising himself as Santa Claus and stealing all the Whos’ toys, food and decorations. Poised to throw it all off a mountain, the grumpy loner has a change of heart as joyous song rises from Whoville.

Industry observers note that “They say that the Grinch’s small heart grew three sizes that day,” giving him “the strength of 10 Grinches plus two,” says the narrator of the 1966 movie version. With a beatific smile, he pulls the stolen goods back from the brink and returns everything.

Would a too-small heart make you grumpy like the Grinch? And what would happen if your heart went from too small to really significant in an instant? The answer depends on what causes the heart to shrink or swell, experts say. And whether or not you are a snake.

Sources indicate that heart size is generally pegged to body size, notes Michelle Kittleson, a cardiologist at Cedars Sinai Smidt Heart Institute in Los Angeles. Bigger people tend to have bigger hearts. But some people, she says, have hearts that are naturally bigger or smaller than average for their bodies. It’s not clear why. However, she says, “there are negative consequences of having a too-small heart.”.

In one 2025 study, researchers looked at medical records from more than 360,000 people in Australia. Those with smaller-than-average hearts had a higher risk of dying within five years than people with average or larger hearts, the team reported in JACC: Advances.

Smaller hearts may not pump blood as well as larger ones, making it harder for people to exercise. And if the Grinch didn’t exercise enough, maybe “then that made him really tired, and that made him grumpy,” Kittleson says. “Or maybe he did the research, and he found out that his life expectancy was shortened because of it, and that made him even grumpier.”.

But would rapidly increasing his heart’s size be good for the Grinch?

As the Grinch slides downhill toward Whoville, pulled by a sled piled high with presents he’d stolen and now was returning, he physically undergoes a change. What started as a heart two sizes too small swelled three sizes, both curing his grumpiness and giving him super strength. Or so the classic tale goes. A person going through such a dramatic change may not fare as well.

Industry observers note that there are many ways a heart can grow, says Leslie Leinwand, a molecular biologist and geneticist at the University of Colorado Boulder. With vigorous exercise, “your heart gets bigger in good ways,” Leinwand says. That can be true for athletes who do lots of cardio, such as swimmers and marathon runners.

According to recent reports, “Their heart gets bigger and thicker,” Kittleson claims. “But it’s a good thing in them because it helps them pump more blood per minute than someone with a normal-size heart.” Pregnancy also makes the whole organ expand to boost blood to the developing fetus. If people stop exercising, or give birth, their hearts will shrink back to normal size within months.

Some diseases, though, can enlarge hearts in deadly ways. “If you’ve got untreated high blood pressure,” Leinwand states, “you can get a huge heart, and it’s not good for you.”.

In a recent development, stress, bad heart valves and some genetic diseases can also result in bigger, but weaker, hearts. In those cases, the heart muscle grows in order to pump more blood. At the same time, the inside of the left ventricle — the heart chamber that pumps oxygenated blood to the body — can shrink. That makes it harder for the heart to push blood out. This kind of growth takes time, Kittleson notes.

In a recent development, there is one rare condition in which the heart can inflate suddenly. Called takotsubo or stress cardiomyopathy — or in some cases, broken-heart syndrome — it is brought on by extreme stress. That can include positive things like winning the lottery or entering a surprise party or negative stress such as break-up or losing a job.

According to recent reports, A surge of epinephrine, or adrenaline, from stress can make the left ventricle bulge into the shape of a pot used to catch octopuses. (Takotsubo is Japanese for “octopus pot.”) That causes immediate heart failure as the heart chamber gets too significant to pump blood.

So instead of becoming super strong, the Grinch “would have keeled over and collapsed,” Kittleson says. (People can survive with prompt medical care and their hearts can return to normal size in a few months.).

Given the Grinch survived his rapid growth, there’s another possible scenario: Maybe his heart is more like a snake’s.

Pythons’ hearts can balloon by up to 25 percent in a day after the snakes eat a large meal — sometimes as big as an adult deer. And the bigger a python’s meal, the more its heart grows. Larger hearts pump blood with more force, Leinwand and her colleagues reported in 2024 in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The researchers don’t know if this makes the snakes stronger overall.

Once a meal is digested, the heart shrinks again. Snakes can go through many shrink-and-grow cycles with no ill effect. Leinwand hopes that studying these snakes will lead to treatments that make human hearts healthier.

But becoming kinder, like the Grinch? Maybe not.

Notes Leinwand, “our snakes, when they eat a lot, they get rather aggressive.”.

By Anna Mattson and Science News Staff.

Science News staff devoured books of all kinds this year, on topics ranging from ecology and evolution to the human brain and mathematics. We covered it all — even a cookbook! These 10 titles rose to the top of our 2026 reading list and could make great gifts for the book lovers in your life. —  Anna Mattson, Assistant Editor.

According to recent reports, substantial thinkers will love Huge Numbers, a fascinating look into the study of large numbers. “When I think of big numbers, I usually think of a 1 with a lot of zeroes tacked on the end. But the reality is much more complex than I ever imagined,” says senior physics writer Emily Conover. The book, among Conover’s favorites of the year, “provided me with a upcoming appreciation of our number system and the creative ways mathematicians have expanded it to express ever-larger numbers,” she says. “Plus, contemplating unfathomably large figures makes my own concerns seem insignificant.”.

Recent findings suggest that staff writer Erin Garcia de Jesús’ favorite book of 2026, The Creatures’ Guide to Caring, will strike a chord with upcoming parents. “Between sleepless nights and poopy diapers, there’s not much to laugh about in the early days of parenting. But I found plenty of humor (and plenty to be grossed out about) in The Creatures’ Guide to Caring,” Garcia de Jesús says. “It’s the perfect book to make anyone, parent or otherwise, feel better that we’re not the only animals struggling with our offspring.”.

Industry observers note that merritt R. TuretskyW.W. Norton & Manufacturer | $29.99.

Adventure seekers will lose themselves in the mesmerizing ecosystems at the heart of Bogland, biomedical sciences writer Aimee Cunningham’s favorite book of the year. Ecologist Merritt R. Turetsky immerses readers in these waterlogged landscapes that are often overlooked and underestimated. “I am firmly on team boglands after reading about the beauty and wonder of these ecosystems,” Cunningham notes.

Saul Justin NewmanThe MIT Press | $29.95.

Senior writer Meghan Rosen’s favorite book of 2026 is perfect for anyone interested in — or wary of — health and wellness culture. Morbid exposes the lack of science behind a lot of antiaging advice, such as eating like centenarians do and taking “anti­aging” supplements. “Turns out, a lot of it is just plain bunk,” Rosen says. “Skeptical readers will enjoy Newman’s takedowns, which go down smoothly with a healthy dose of humor.”.

Susana CarmonaThe MIT Press | $27.95.

Industry observers note that senior neuroscience writer Laura Sanders’ pick for 2026 is a must-read for any expecting mother, fresh mother or person looking to learn about how pregnancy and motherhood impact the body. “A Mother’s Brain reads like a scientific love letter to moms, who all too often get overlooked,” she states. Author and neuroscientist Susana Carmona “covers the nascent field of matrescence in lively, vivid chapters. And along the way, she convincingly argues that the maternal brain is compelling, wondrous and still mysterious,” Sanders says.

Aaron MahnkeRunning Press | $30.00.

In a recent development, those who listen to true crime podcasts or wish spooky season lasted all year long will enjoy Exhumed, an exploration of the lore and medical practices leading up to the 19th century Latest England vampire panic. “Thanks to Mahnke’s gripping prose, I felt like I was in the middle of the action. It was hard to lay the book down,” assistant editor Anna Mattson wrote in her online review. Mattson notes that Exhumed, her favorite read of 2026, is littered with bizarre facts that would be perfect for invigorating dull conversations.

For the anthropologist in your life, try The Story of Stories — a deep dive into how technological upheavals have shaped storytelling throughout history. The author provides what Sanders describes as scattershot history lessons in her online review: “Ashton has a knack for pulling out memorable bits from historical records, scientific studies and other sources for readers.”.

Alexis Nikole NelsonSimon & Schuster | $35.00.

Conover couldn’t pick just one favorite. For people who enjoy getting creative in the kitchen, she recommends Happy Snacking, Don’t Die! “This cookbook provides such a joyful how-to on foraging and eating wild plants,” Conover states. “It helped me see my plant neighbors in a whole new light. And I got to make some tasty treats to share with my family as well.”.

Riley BlackSt. Martin’s Press | $29.00.

Tyrant Lizard Queen is the only work of fiction on our list. But it’s rooted in real science, and stars a Tyrannosaurus rex. Author Riley Black “offers an empathetic look at a real-life creature that experienced hunger and pain, much like the animals that surround us today,” says Science News Explores assistant editor Aaron Tremper, who chose the book as his favorite of 2026. “Black’s penchant for story makes for a thrilling read that fans of Jurassic Park and King Kong can get behind.”.

Industry observers note that joshua D. MezrichThe MIT Press | $29.95.

November 19: Mercury moves into Libra.

Sources indicate that the Moon passes 5° north of Neptune at 8 A.M. EST; 12 hours later, our satellite passes 7° north of Saturn at 8 P.M. EST. The trio is visible in the southeastern sky two hours after sunset, forming a triangle with the Moon to the upper left of Saturn, and Neptune to Saturn’s right. Only the Moon and Saturn are visible to the naked eye, while Neptune will require optical aid.

From the gibbous Moon, drop down first to check out Saturn through a telescope, including its lovely ring system and brightest moon, Titan. Saturn is the brightest object in this part of the sky after the Moon, so you don’t have to worry about misidentifying it. After passing south of the ringed world earlier this week, Titan now sits about 3.2’ to Saturn’s west, in line with the rings. Fainter moons Tethys, Rhea, and Dione may be visible clustered closer to the planet, but the bright moonlight might also make them challenging for visual observation.

According to recent reports, from Saturn, scan 6.6° west-southwest to land on Neptune. If you have a go-to scope, it may take you right to the outermost planet, which glows at magnitude 7.7 and offers up a tiny, 2”-wide disk. It may look like a “flat,” bluish-gray star, rather than a bright pinprick of white light. Look for a large parallelogram of 4th- and 5th-magnitude stars just over 9° to Saturn’s southwest if you need a closer stepping stone. The star at the northeastern point of that shape is 5th-magnitude 29 Piscium, and it lies about 2.6° southwest of Neptune.

Thune will lead Republicans through the minority
