#65662. Breaking: Scientists Studied Thousands of Ancient Skeletons and Found a Strange Truth About Human Progress

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (768 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popularmechanics ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Scientists Studied Thousands of Ancient Skeletons and Found a Strange Truth About Human Progress

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (768 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It does a body good” slogan has some historical backing, at least in Europe.
  • In a recent development, “When children and adolescents have access to sufficient, high-quality food, they grow taller, within the constraints of genetic factors,” Manon Stephan, an economic historian at Germany’s University of Tübingen, said in a statement.
  • To test that idea, Stephan and colleagues at Tübingen and the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology examined 18,457 bones from 783 sites in 45 countries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The dairy industry’s “Milk. It does a body good” slogan has some historical backing, at least in Europe. That’s one of the more surprising takeaways from a large study that used ancient skeletons to track how well people lived across Europe and Asia over the past 7,000 years. The researchers based their analysis on one telling measurement: human height.

In a recent development, “When children and adolescents have access to sufficient, high-quality food, they grow taller, within the constraints of genetic factors,” Manon Stephan, an economic historian at Germany’s University of Tübingen, said in a statement. “Therefore, height enables us to draw conclusions about living standards.”.

To test that idea, Stephan and colleagues at Tübingen and the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology examined 18,457 bones from 783 sites in 45 countries. In the study, published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the team estimated people’s heights from their long bones. They then tracked how average height changed in each region and compared those changes with shifts in population density and technology.

Industry observers note that in China, men were taller 7,000 years ago, averaging 5 feet 10 inches. Over time, however, their height steadily declined, reaching a low of just 5 feet 3 inches on average in the 19th century. Chinese women’s height also declined, though less drastically, falling from an average of 5 feet 2 inches 7,000 years ago to 4 feet 10 inches in more recent times.

Trends like these would be nearly impossible to trace through written records alone. “In many parts of the world, any written sources that would allow us to draw conclusions about economic development appear quite late on our timeline and are patchy in their distribution,” Stephan mentioned. “That’s why we rely on bones.” The bones in question came from 22 Asian and 23 European countries and were taken from the graves of commoners in both densely populated and rural regions.

In Europe, by contrast, the trends went in a different direction. Around 5,000 years ago, men in northern Europe averaged just 5 feet 4 inches. However, the study authors wrote, as pastoralist peoples migrated from the steppes of Eastern Europe and western Siberia, they brought with them more advanced dairy farming and the genetic trait of lactose tolerance. This led to greater consumption of dairy products, which the study identifies as a leading factor in increased height. Average heights in northern Europe continued to climb into the early Middle Ages, but sometime between 500 and 1000 C.E., they began to decline, a trend that lasted until the end of the 19th century.

Women’s heights followed a similar pattern. China and Japan experienced the steepest declines, while Europe saw a rise, though a less steep one than among men.

Recent findings suggest that the authors wrote that “human stature is a valuable indicator of nutritional status and health.” Reconstructing this indicator offers insight into which societies provided better health and nutrition to their people. Surprisingly, technological progress did not prove to be a major factor in improving either.

It has been revealed that “Our study also confirmed that technological progress does not automatically lead to greater height,” remarked Jörg Baten, a professor of economic history at the University of Tübingen. “In China, for example, fresh, higher-yielding rice varieties and other innovations were introduced in the 11th century [C.E.]. While the higher yields enabled the empire to remain the dominant power, they did not subsequently lead to a better standard of living for the general population. Instead, population density increased: People had more children because this was seen as a form of security in old age. This meant, however, that each individual had not more to eat, but less. And importantly the quality declined, for example, in terms of high-quality protein.”.

It has been revealed that europe’s findings on technology mirrored Asia’s. Improved technology helped support denser populations, but it didn’t increase average height or necessarily improve the nutritional value of food.

Industry observers note that going forward, the authors hope to link more of these changes in height to shifts in social conditions or developments in agriculture. “This requires further research,” said Mark Hudson, an archaeologist at the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology. “However, the statistical data reveal trends and provide clues as to when these changes occurred.”.

Tim Newcomb is a journalist based in the Pacific Northwest. He covers stadiums, sneakers, gear, infrastructure, and more for a variety of publications, including Popular Mechanics. His favorite interviews have included sit-downs with Roger Federer in Switzerland, Kobe Bryant in Los Angeles, and Tinker Hatfield in Portland.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Rand Paul, R-Ky., leaves the Senate Republicans’ lunch in the Capitol on Tuesday.
  • Rand Paul, R-Ky., announced Wednesday he looks to serve as the top Republican on the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee when Democrats take control of Congress next year.
  • The move clears the way for Senate Ethics Chairman James Lankford, R-Okla., to use his seniority to ascend to ranking Republican on the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which Paul currently chairs, and touches off several other shifts at the top of other committees.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., leaves the Senate Republicans’ lunch in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., announced Wednesday he looks to serve as the top Republican on the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee when Democrats take control of Congress next year.

The move clears the way for Senate Ethics Chairman James Lankford, R-Okla., to use his seniority to ascend to ranking Republican on the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which Paul currently chairs, and touches off several other shifts at the top of other committees.

It has been revealed that the move fit in with Sen. Lisa Murkowski’s bid to use her seniority to succeed Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, as top Republican on the Appropriations panel. If Paul did not go to the top spot on HELP, Murkowski, R-Alaska, would be next in line for that committee in the next Congress.

Murkowski is second in seniority on Appropriations to Collins, who was defeated for reelection. But she faces a potential challenge from Sen. Jerry Moran, R-Kan., who is next in line behind her.

Paul mentioned in a press release that he prepares to bring the same approach to the HELP Committee as he did as chairman of Homeland, where he said he “challenged entrenched bureaucracies, forced federal officials to answer for their actions, and pulled back the curtain on what Washington tried to keep hidden.”.

It has been revealed that he cited calling Dr. Anthony Fauci before the committee to probe the former federal health official’s role in pandemic-related shutdowns and the origin of the COVID-19 virus, and releasing thousands of pages of pandemic-related documents. Paul, an ophthalmologist, said at HELP he will “stand against efforts to put Washington between Americans and their doctors, their children’s schools, and their paychecks.” He predicted “a rush toward socialism unlike anything we have seen” when the Democrat-controlled Congress convenes in January.

Lankford, in a separate statement, confirmed his interest in becoming the ranking member of the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee. In many areas, he stated, the panel can work in a bipartisan manner, and over the past decade he “worked across the aisle to improve emergency communications in federal buildings, strengthen the United States Postal Service, increase federal cybersecurity preparedness, government transparency, and the use of artificial intelligence.”.

Sources indicate that but he added that his job also would be to “push back on a [Democratic] majority that goes too far . . . Oversight is responsible, but obstruction is unacceptable.”.

Recent findings suggest that lankford noted he would work together with the likely committee chair, Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., “when we can agree and be a fierce opposition if there is an attempt to undercut our nation’s security.”.

Industry News: The Secret Reason Why Ancient Roman Concrete Is So Remarkably Strong—And How One Engineer Has Recreated It

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1023 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.
  • According to recent reports, the Pantheon, Rome’s unreinforced concrete dome, constructed around 118 to 125 C.E., still stands intact to this day.
  • For decades, researchers credited the inclusion of volcanic ash from Pozzuoli, a city in Naples, Italy, for the unique strength in the mix; others claimed that lime, a calcium oxide or calcium hydroxide binder created from heating limestone, was the key ingredient.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.

According to recent reports, the Pantheon, Rome’s unreinforced concrete dome, constructed around 118 to 125 C.E., still stands intact to this day. The Aqua Virgo, part of the ancient Roman system of aqueducts, was built in 19 B.C.E., yet still supplies Roman fountains, including Trevi, today. Is it any wonder that ancient Rome still draws our global admiration?

For decades, researchers credited the inclusion of volcanic ash from Pozzuoli, a city in Naples, Italy, for the unique strength in the mix; others claimed that lime, a calcium oxide or calcium hydroxide binder created from heating limestone, was the key ingredient. Massachusetts Institute of Technology’s Admir Masic, a civil and environmental engineering professor, thought there must be more to the story.

Sources indicate that masic established a lab at MIT with the specific goal of researching ancient Roman concrete. First and foremost a chemist, he notes he knew there was something beneath the surface of Roman concrete potentially lending it strength. His team of researchers, from MIT, Harvard, Italy, and Switzerland, discovered that ancient Roman concrete gets its strength—and therefore its incredible longevity—from its inherent self-healing properties. As cracks form, the surrounding material somehow fills them back in, over and over.

Sources indicate that scientists commonly suspected that ash, and not lime, was the hero of the Roman concrete-making process, because the Romans were the first to add volcanic ash to the mixture. This hydration-based method gives the mixture additional strength and makes it possible to build in all seasons.

In a recent development, but it didn’t explain the self-healing quality. Another mystery was in the concrete’s apparent crystalline phases, known to take shape only at high temperatures—at least 80 degrees Celsius (or about 176 degrees Fahrenheit). Yet, the Romans wouldn’t have exposed their concrete mixture to those sorts of temperatures.

In a recent development, then, researchers discovered calcium aluminate hydrate being used as a binding agent in ancient Roman concrete, which only created further intrigue. This is where the mystery of self-healing gained its first significant clue—trying to learn where the calcium came from, Masic indicates. So his team’s focus shifted to the overlooked role of lime, which is primarily composed of calcium compounds.

According to recent reports, masic notes that modern concrete, when mixed with lime, volcanic components, and water, creates a homogeneous mixture—quite unlike ancient Roman concrete, which is studded with tiny, distinct white particles. “How is it possible that every construction site would make this heterogeneous material even though they put so much effort [into] making it very standard in terms of ingredients [and] how to mix it?” Masic wondered.

According to recent reports, the research team decided to investigate the mechanical, structural, and chemical properties of these particles, dubbed “lime clasts,” which were present in every sample they analyzed, Masic indicates. It led the team to realize “that lime clasts are not an error in mixing, or sloppy mixing, but they are the root of a very specific way of mixing mortars.” Not present in modern concrete, but ubiquitous in the ancient Roman version.

Originally, researchers believed that the Romans added water to the lime mixture to make a slurry. This “slaking” creates a homogeneously structured mixture. However, the presence of the lime clasts didn’t fit into this model.

What the Romans actually did was “hot mixing,” which introduces a novel series of chemical reactions. They ground the stone into tiny pieces of calcium oxide and mixed them with volcanic ash and a dry aggregate. Finally, they added water. “This is where the reaction of calcium oxide with water happens, and the entire mix gets hot, [which] releases energy, and creates hot spots up to 200 to 250 degrees Celsius,” Masic explains.

While lime and the ash formed the basis of the mixture, the constellation of millimeter-scale, mineral particles embedded throughout the mortar turned out to be the secret outcome of the hot mixing process. The key to hot mixing is that it doesn’t dissolve all of the lime clasts. Instead, they get systematically embedded into the concrete mix, creating a reservoir of calcium. When the concrete is exposed to water, the calcium spontaneously expands, creating a protective layer of nanoparticles that fill in the cracks before they can spread. Voila, self-healing concrete. Masic’s team published their findings in the journal Science Advances.

The team’s own recreation of Roman concrete healed a crack within two weeks. A modern concrete mixture didn’t heal at all, allowing water to flow through the crack. Eventually, water seepage like this destroys the integrity of modern concrete structures.

Roman self-healing concrete allows the mixture to last longer and requires less maintenance and less fresh material for construction—which also reduces emissions during concrete production. Standard cement production, the solid binder in concrete, accounts for about 8 percent of global CO2 emissions today.

According to recent reports, our world actually has various forms of self-healing concrete, such as bioconcrete, in which bacterial spores activate and produce calcium carbonate to fill in cracks. However, the high costs of modern methods keep the industry from using them widely, claims Masic. Meanwhile the ancient Roman method offers “self-healing at an extremely competitive price,” he says.

Now that we know the secret, should we return to making concrete this way?

In a recent development, in fact, Masic co-founded a tech giant in 2021, that uses lessons he has learned from studying ancient Roman concrete. Today, DMAT is creating a concrete additive “that increases the lifespan of concrete structures by 50 percent and reduces CO2 emissions to 40% of traditional concrete,” according to MIT’s Climate Portal. As of August 2026, their material is part of underground water tanks, road barriers, and pavement in Italy and Switzerland. DMAT also intends to expand to U.S. infrastructure projects.

Manasee Wagh contributed to this story.

Tim Newcomb is a journalist based in the Pacific Northwest. He covers stadiums, sneakers, gear, infrastructure, and more for a variety of publications, including Popular Mechanics. His favorite interviews have included sit-downs with Roger Federer in Switzerland, Kobe Bryant in Los Angeles, and Tinker Hatfield in Portland.

Scott Colom elected Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (751 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that mississippi Democrat Scott Colom, here at a news conference in Jackson on Nov.
  • Democrat Scott Colom has unseated Republican Sen.
  • The result is a stunning flip for Democrats in a deep-red state where they last won a Senate election in 1982, and it brings the Senate Democratic Caucus to at least 55 seats in the next Congress.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that mississippi Democrat Scott Colom, here at a news conference in Jackson on Nov. 4, has defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. (Rogelio V. Solis/Getty Images).

Democrat Scott Colom has unseated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith to become Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction.

The result is a stunning flip for Democrats in a deep-red state where they last won a Senate election in 1982, and it brings the Senate Democratic Caucus to at least 55 seats in the next Congress.

It has been revealed that colom was leading Hyde-Smith 49.2 percent to 48.7 percent — or by just over 4,600 votes out of more than 960,000 cast — when The Associated Press called the race Wednesday, a little over a week after Election Day. Ty Pinkins, the 2024 Democratic Senate nominee who ran as an independent this year, had 2 percent.

In recent days, as absentee and provisional ballots were counted, Colom had all but declared victory, repeatedly saying that Hyde-Smith had no path to victory.

“I'll work every day in the U.S. Senate to build a future that generations of Mississippians can be just as proud to call home,” he posted Monday on social media.

With his victory, Colom joins several other Democrats who flipped seats in deep-red states, including Texas’ James Talarico, Kansas’ Adam Hamilton and South Carolina’s Annie Andrews. Democrats have so far flipped eight Senate seats to win control of the chamber, overcoming a difficult Senate map and giving them their largest majority in the chamber since 2011.

It has been revealed that that majority could expand further if Democrats flip the Senate seat in Alaska, where former Rep. Mary Peltola narrowly leads Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan.

Republicans have dominated Senate elections in Mississippi in recent decades. The last Democrat to be elected senator in the Magnolia State was John C. Stennis, who won his sixth full and final term in 1982. Colom will be the third Black man to serve as a Mississippi senator after Republicans Hiram Revels and Blanche Bruce during Reconstruction.

While Revels and Bruce, who left office in 1881, were elected by the state Legislature, Colom will be the first Black senator elected directly by voters.

Colom has served as a district attorney for four counties in northeast Mississippi since 2016. President Joe Biden nominated him for a federal district judgeship in 2022, but Hyde-Smith effectively blocked his nomination by not returning a so-called blue slip, a Senate Judiciary Committee tradition that lets senators derail district judge nominees in their home states.

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer noted last week that he’d had Colom in his sights for several years as a potential Senate candidate, including for a race against the state’s senior senator, Republican Roger Wicker.

“I had Scott Colom and his father come to my house, and I served them a nice little brunch or something. I said, ‘You got to run,’” the Upcoming York Democrat recalled to MS NOW. “They were smarter than me. This was four years ago. They said, ‘We don’t want to run this time, but we know that Hyde-[Smith], the incumbent, is so weak, we could beat her.’”.

Still, the Mississippi race didn’t capture as much national attention as other Senate contests until the closing weeks of the campaign. A trio of Black senators, Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland, Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware and Cory Booker of Upcoming Jersey, all campaigned with Colom throughout the summer and fall. Key national figures, including former President Bill Clinton, former Vice President Kamala Harris and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, also stumped for him in October.

In a recent development, colom’s campaign engaged voters with quirky ads and unconventional forms of outreach, including meeting with people lining up to attend a Trump rally. One ad that went viral played on Hyde Smith saying earlier this year that people had “so many proteins to choose from” when asked about rising beef prices.

It has been revealed that “Pick another protein?” says a man in the ad. “I’d rather pick another senator instead.”.

It has been revealed that major Democratic outside groups made a late play in the state, with WinSenate, which is affiliated with Senate Democrats’ top super PAC, investing $2.2 million. The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee spent $500,000 on a coordinated ad buy late last month.

According to recent reports, the pro-Republican Senate Leadership Fund dropped $1.7 million on the race, and Trump headlined a rally for Hyde-Smith on Oct. 26.

The Odyssey of the Seas has returned to its homeport in the Upcoming York region for a winter season offering cruises to the Bahamas and the Caribbean.

Having completed a seasonal deployment in the Eastern Mediterranean and the Greek Islands, the Royal Caribbean vessel arrived in Cape Liberty on November 8, 2026.

Before kicking off its winter season, the 2021-built vessel operated a trans-Atlantic crossing that started in Civitavecchia, Italy.

The 14-night repositioning voyage included visits to destinations in Spain and Portugal.

Odyssey’s New York season starts with a series of seven-night cruises to the Bahamas and Florida, which sail to Nassau and Port Canaveral.

The itineraries are also highlighted by visits to Royal Caribbean’s private island destination of Perfect Day at CocoCay.

Recent findings suggest that starting in January, the vessel will also offer longer cruises to the Eastern Caribbean, operating 11- and 12-night cruises to ports of call that include Bridgetown in Barbados, Charlotte Amalie in St. Thomas and St. John’s in Antigua.

The season runs through late April, when the Odyssey of the Seas is scheduled to embark on a repositioning voyage back to Europe.

Sailing from Cape Liberty to Civitavecchia, the 14-night cruise will feature visits to destinations in Portugal, Spain and Italy, including Ponta Delgada, Málaga, Cartagena and La Spezia.

The ship is scheduled to embark on another summer season in the Mediterranean in early November, offering weeklong cruises to the Greek Islands and Italy.

Completing five years of service in 2026, the Odyssey of the Seas underwent a routine drydock before its summer season.

The 4,200-passenger vessel underwent technical maintenance during the shipyard stay, in addition to overall upkeep work on public areas and staterooms.

Built at the Meyer Werft shipyard in Papenburg, Germany, the ship is part of Royal Caribbean’s Quantum-class series.

Some Democrats doubt Trump is serious about cutting deals in fresh Congress

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1050 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • President Donald Trump speaks with reporters on the South Lawn of the White House on Oct.
  • President Donald Trump’s postelection statements about working with Democrats have presented the incoming majority with a kaleidoscope to decipher, but some Democratic lawmakers have their doubts.
  • On the one hand, the Republican president has contended that he can work with House and Senate Democrats after the fresh Congress is seated in January, even floating a bipartisan immigration bill.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

President Donald Trump speaks with reporters on the South Lawn of the White House on Oct. 13 before leaving for a campaign rally in Alaska. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

President Donald Trump’s postelection statements about working with Democrats have presented the incoming majority with a kaleidoscope to decipher, but some Democratic lawmakers have their doubts.

On the one hand, the Republican president has contended that he can work with House and Senate Democrats after the fresh Congress is seated in January, even floating a bipartisan immigration bill. But on the other, he promoted his hard-line aide Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff, raising doubts about any cooling of the political environment.

At every stop along his October campaign rally blitz before Republicans suffered massive losses on Nov. 3, Trump railed against “Dumbocrats” and their “bad” policies. He mocked their candidates as too extreme, too corrupt and too beholden to the most progressive wing of their party. He even warned that, if voters handed them control of the House and Senate, it would set off “a 1929-style economic depression.”.

Recent findings suggest that voters ignored him. They handed House Democrats over 250 seats at least come January, and the party will have at least 54 seats in the Senate.

Sources indicate that trump was asked during a “60 Minutes” interview taped Friday afternoon at the White House if he could resist insulting Democratic lawmakers for six months if that’s how long it took to reach a deal on major legislation. “Very easily,” he responded.

But several Democrats are so sure about getting to a “Kumbaya” moment with Trump during his final two years.

Virginia Sen. Tim Kaine said it was hard to take the president at his word because he is “so unpredictable.”.

“But I'm certainly telling my colleagues we should try to put as many bills as we can on his desk that do good things for the American public, and then see how he behaves,” he said Tuesday.

Industry observers note that "We're gonna put bills in front of the president on affordability starting Day One,” California Rep. Robert Garcia, the likely incoming House Oversight and Government Reform chair, said Tuesday. “We'll have to see if he's serious, but I don't trust Donald Trump for a second.”.

The White House on Monday sent Garcia a letter, obtained by CQ Roll Call, warning House Democrats that their anticipated spate of probes "may cross the line into blatant criminality.".

Rep. Jim McGovern, a Massachusetts Democrat who is in line to chair the Rules Committee in the new Congress, noted on the floor Tuesday that he does not see a GOP that is ready to heed the election's lessons and come to the bargaining table.

In a recent development, “Instead of taking the hint or listening to the overwhelming majority of Americans who told them to change course, Republicans are doubling down on the same tactics and messaging they've been jamming down our throats these last two years, and it's a perfect example of why they lost in the first place,” he said. “They do not listen.

Industry observers note that “Then to double down even further, the failed lame-duck president appointed Stephen Miller, the architect of all the cruel policies that most people hate, as his latest White House chief of staff,” McGovern added, referring to the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. “What planet are these people living on?”.

Kaine remarked congressional Democrats might not notice that much of a change from the White House with Miller moving into the chief’s suite near the Oval Office.

“Stephen Miller was calling a lot of the shots, even if he wasn't chief of staff,” the Virginia Democrat said. “So I view that as a kind of a change of the face, but not of the character of the administration.”.

House Republicans’ Tuesday vote to make hard-line conservative Jim Jordan of Ohio their next leader is another red flag for Democrats.

In a recent development, “White House Chief of staff Stephen Miller and House Minority Leader Jim Jordan,” Brendan Duke, a former senior Democratic Senate aide now with the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, wrote on X. “Where is the pivot to the center after a historic election loss?”.

Recent findings suggest that getting to the center is what retiring Nebraska Rep. Don Bacon says his fellow Republicans and Trump should be doing after the election massacre.

"I do wish we could get to the point where we could solve big problems, instead of just beating the other side,” noted Bacon, who has floated a 2028 presidential bid. “We can’t do this Republican-only or Democrat-only. And I would say this to the president, too: We’ve got to start working across the aisle to solve these problems.”.

Sources indicate that despite his postelection talk of working with Democrats, Trump has sought to blame them for an up-and-down U.S. stock market.

It has been revealed that “Right after the election it went down $3 trillion,” he said Monday during an unplanned White House press briefing. “That was because of the result of the election, because the stock market does not want to see Democrats. And your 401(k)s have gone way down because of the ridiculous result.”.

According to recent reports, he's also returned this week to questioning the midterm results: “It's not even a result. It's almost hard to believe. Now, I wasn't on the ballot.”.

Members of House Republicans’ upcoming leadership team on Tuesday sounded dug in and ready for a partisan brawl over Democrats’ promised investigations into the president, many of his top aides and Trump family members. Jordan's election as GOP leader shows that “we are ready to dig in for the fight,” outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson told reporters Tuesday.

Michigan Rep. Lisa McClain, who was reelected House GOP conference chair, pointed to Garcia's two-word statement on Election Day: "Lawyer up.".

“Tell me how ‘lawyering up’ helps anybody with affordability?" she said. “They're going to be focused on going after President Trump. We are going to be focused on improving the quality of life for every American.”.

Sources indicate that to that end, retiring Maryland Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, a former No. 2 House Democrat, said Republicans should heed one big takeaway from the election: “Trump lost.”.

In a recent development, gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

As the weather gets cold, you don’t have to pay an arm and a leg just to keep your limbs from freezing off. Instead of heating your entire home, simply plug in a space heater and get direct warmth from a nearby source. If you want a compact yet powerful option, the Lasko Whirlwind Heat Oscillating Space Heater is an ideal choice.

Industry observers note that what I like so much about this Lasko is its combination of size, power, and oscillation. It is small enough to sit comfortably on my desk or nightstand without taking up too much space, yet in combination with the dual-axis oscillation and powerful heating, it can warm up an entire room.

Much like the Dreo Whole Room Heater, the Lasko is designed with dual-axis oscillation, meaning it oscillates both vertically and horizontally. It can also oscillate in both directions simultaneously for greater coverage of an entire space. As a result, the heater boasts a total coverage of up to 300 square feet, which should be more than enough for most bedrooms, offices, and even many living rooms.

That design is backed by 1,500 watts of heating power. The heat comes at three different heating levels that adjust the fan power. On its highest level, the heating is almost abrasive up close. In a small room at our office, I felt a tangible difference in temperature around the entire room within minutes, and just as importantly, near-instant hot air from the second I turned it on.

My one complaint is that there isn’t a separate control for both heat levels and fan power, which could lead to a slightly more nuanced level of control. That said, the auto-eco mode allows you to set a specific temperature, which the space heater will reach, go on low heat mode until it is two degrees above the set temperature, and then shut off automatically.

This makes it a lot easier to run without direct supervision or accidentally running it for hours on end. Similarly, there is a sleep mode as well where you can set a timer up to 12 hours so it will shut off after a set amount of time, making it great to use once you get in bed.

The Lasko packs all that power in a relatively compact body. In cases of cold streaks in my drafty office building, I can set it up to run on my desk without feeling like I’ve sacrificed all my working space just to stay warm. In fact, I can still have my laptop, books, and assorted gear strewn about.

Recent findings suggest that placed on the nightstand or on top of a dresser, it works perfectly to warm you up from bed as well. One of the small but notable features is the remote control. While not uncommon, I also love the remote control. I can place it on a stand or even in the corner of a room when I don’t want direct heat and still control the heat level, temperature setting, oscillation, sleep timer, and screen light.

The Lasko Whirlwind doesn’t have any specifically unique safety features, but it has everything you might need for peace of mind. The ceramic safety plug can handle high levels of wattage without overheating to prevent electrical fires, and the space heater will automatically shut off if the motor overheats or the body tips over. The overall housing surrounding the heater stays cool, so you won’t burn your hands if you need to touch it.

Industry observers note that the Lasko Whirlwind does exactly what I want it to. I want powerful heat, customizable temperature settings, and quality safety features, and the Lasko provides that. The small size takes that powerful heat and puts it in a container that is compact enough to fit on desks, nightstands, or in the corner of your room.

Industry observers note that if you want a device powerful enough to heat up a full room but small enough to fit anywhere, the Lasko Whirlwind is an excellent choice. If you want to heat up large spaces, you might need something a bit larger, but very few space heaters have pound for pound as much power as this one.

#65643. The 6 Best Mini-LED TVs Deliver a Bright Screen and Great Value

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (3015 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popularmechanics ↗ Open Full Page

The 6 Best Mini-LED TVs Deliver a Bright Screen and Great Value

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3015 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Mini-LED is among the most versatile display technologies ever created.
  • The best mini-LED TVs right now provide a brighter and more impactful picture than ever, especially since many of them get a performance boost from other display tech like quantum dots and the hot new multicolored backlight configuration, RGB LED.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Mini-LED is among the most versatile display technologies ever created. By shrinking down the LED backlighting that powered older TVs since flat screens first gained traction in the late 2000s, TV makers have found a way to deliver brighter TVs with richer, more accurate colors without relying on expensive new display technologies.

The best mini-LED TVs right now provide a brighter and more impactful picture than ever, especially since many of them get a performance boost from other display tech like quantum dots and the hot new multicolored backlight configuration, RGB LED.

Sources indicate that just as importantly, they often offer great bang for the buck, especially when you're looking for a larger screen size—let’s say 75 inches or higher. As malleable as they are cost-effective, mini-LED is the secret sauce behind some of the best TVs on the market, even outdoing premium OLED screens in metrics like brightness and color expansion.

We’ve tested the top mini-LED TVs around, from entry-level options to groundbreaking flagships, to help you find the best options for your money.

Recent findings suggest that I picked the top mini-LED TVs after sampling the best the market has to offer from brands like LG, Samsung, Sony, TCL, and Hisense. I tested four of the TVs directly, while two of them were tested by Popular Mechanics staff and recommended based on that testing.

Sources indicate that my evaluation was based on performance traits like brightness, color vibrancy and accuracy, image processing and upscaling, black levels, and overall contrast. For my testing process, I used objective measurements like brightness and color accuracy with a Portrait Displays C6 HDR5000 colorimeter, a G1 pattern generator, and Calman software, as well as subjective testing using a wide library of familiar content, from test demos to films and TV highlights via 4K HDR Blu-rays and streaming. I also weighed usability features like smarts and gaming options, overall design, and size options for those interested in the ever-expanding big-screen TV market.

It has been revealed that I’ve been reviewing TVs and audio technology for well over a decade at publications like Wired, Business Insider, Digital Trends, and others. I’ve reviewed virtually every kind of TV and display technology available, from budget screens to premium RGB LEDs. I’ve gone hands-on with the best new mini-LED TVs from brands like Samsung, LG, Sony, TCL, Hisense, Roku, and others, along with competing tech like OLED and QD-OLED, each of which has its advantages. Few things give me more pleasure than finding people the best tech for their money at every performance level and budget.

RGB LED, which uses tri-colored red, green, and blue light clusters for enhanced color expression, was the hot new display tech at the start of 2026. Virtually every major brand debuted some form of RGB Mini-LED, kick-starting a premium Mini-LED alternative to OLED.

When TCL introduced its own RGB TV for 2026, the RM9L, it seemed less excited about the RGB factor, and more interested in hyping up its exclusive new mini-LED tech, Super Quantum Dots (SQD). The QM8L makes it easy to see why.

SQD is an advanced version of regular quantum dots: tiny nanocrystals that emit pure, bright colors when exposed to light to enhance colors and brightness. Fancy tech aside, the results speak for themselves. The QM8L offers incredible brightness, far outshining its predecessor, the QM8K, alongside expansive colors that are as accurate as they are vibrant.

Recent findings suggest that the upcoming display offers other benefits, including fantastic black levels with very little light bleed, and reduced off-angle performance loss for most settings. Image processing has also improved, getting closer to the clarity and upscaling in top flagships from brands like LG and Samsung. The result is a premium picture that comes tantalizingly close to OLED displays in terms of contrast between the lightest and darkest images, and details that seem to pull you into the screen.

Sources indicate that the TV’s Google TV interface is another plus, offering easy setup and extras like the ability to add albums from your Google Photos library as screen savers. Modern connectivity provides top-tier gaming features across inputs, and the sound isn’t bad either, thanks to built-in Bang & Olufsen speakers. Given that you can grab a 65-inch QM8L for as low as $1,000 or less on sale, it’s an easy pick for the best mini-LED TV available.

Industry observers note that in many ways, entry-level TVs like the Hisense U6SF Pro are the best way to gauge how far TV tech has come in recent years. You just don’t expect a TV this cheap to look this good, from punchy brightness and naturalistic colors to minimal light bleed that lets you watch even challenging scenes in a dark room without being pulled out of the moment.

One sacrifice at this price is the TV’s black levels, which don’t look as rich as pricier mini-LED TVs, let alone self-lit OLED displays. Because of that, even though the TV’s brightness rises above anything you can stream, it can look less striking than step-up models. On the other hand, its matte-like screen does a great job of diminishing ambient light and even direct light reflections for a good picture day or night. That’s something I didn’t expect to see at this level.

Sources indicate that you’ll get some handy features, including support for all major HDR formats and dual HDMI 2.1 ports with VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) up to 144 Hz for PC gaming, another impressive get at this price. I find the TV’s Fire TV smart system a little clunky, but it includes some cool extras, like Ambient Mode that displays free artwork. TCL’s QM6K is a good alternative thanks to its friendlier Google TV smart system, but it can’t match the U6SF Pro’s performance, which is the best I’ve tested at its price point.

The step-down model of our top-rated QM8L, TCL’s QM7L offers many of the same goodies that make its pricier sibling such a rock star, but at a much lower list price. It all starts with the same SQD display tech, for excellent brightness and color vibrancy, and the kind of dimensional contrast that pushes mini-LED closer to OLED.

Industry observers note that the QM7L isn’t quite as much of a powerhouse as the QM8L, but it’s still put-on-your-sunglasses bright, blasting well past anything you can stream, and properly lighting high-quality 4K HDR Blu-rays. Its potency aids in remarkable color expansion for a deep dive into advanced films like Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse. Importantly, the TV also provides good color accuracy, along with deep black levels for excellent contrast. You’ll still see some minor light bleed if you look for it, and picture quality is reduced off-axis, but both are relatively minor concessions, especially for the price.

Sources indicate that the TV offers a similarly loaded set of gaming features to last year’s QM7K, including options like VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) and ALLM (Auto Low Latency Mode) across two of its four HDMI inputs. Like the QM8L, its Google TV smart system is intuitive to set up and use. That’s all icing on a TV that comes about as close as I’ve seen to a premium display for the money.

Hisense’s mid-tier mini-LED TV doesn’t offer the latest display technologies like RGB LED or Super Quantum Dots, but it does offer seriously punchy performance, along with a design that feels much more premium than its price class suggests. That starts with Hisense’s latest anti-reflective matte screen that eliminates most ambient reflections, matched by slim bezels and a stylish pedestal stand with the kind of build quality usually reserved for flagship TVs.

Under the hood is a potent mini-LED display that employs regular quantum dots for rich colors and brightness that meets or beats anything in its class, including TCL’s QM7L. When paired with its rich black levels and reflection-repelling screen, you’ll have no trouble watching even darker reveals in a bright room. Hisense’s image processing has also improved for enhanced detail and upscaling with low-quality content. I did notice that the TV’s local dimming may create some artifacts at its highest setting, but it’s a very minor issue. Like most backlit TVs, it also loses some picture quality when viewed from an angle.

Feature-wise, the U7SG is a gaming master, including VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) at up to 165 Hz across all four HDMI inputs, and handy extras like an intuitive game bar for adjusting settings on the fly. Add in its snappy Google TV interface, and you’re getting a whole lot of good stuff at a price that often falls well below $1,000 for a 65-inch model, and stays competitive up to a whopping 116 inches.

After skipping a year, Hisense’s flagship U9 series is back, now loaded with the latest RGB LED display tech for a striking makeover. The TV uses its tri-colored red, green, and blue mini-LED backlighting to great effect, providing rich black levels and sparkling colors that increasingly close the gap with OLED, alongside the kind of dazzling brightness that OLED can’t yet match.

The UR9’s screen gets an advanced version of Hisense’s matte-like anti-glare coating called “Obsidian,” which impressively repels ambient and even most direct light sources, making it a great option in sunlit rooms. Turn the lights off, and you’ll find great shadow detail and very little light bleed from bright objects on dark backgrounds.

Sources indicate that hisense outfits the TV with some premium extras, from a capable 4.1.2-channel speaker system to HDMI 2.1 support at up to 165 Hz across all three HDMI inputs. There’s also a DisplayPort for connecting a PC, though I would have liked to see a fourth HDMI 2.1 port as well. The TV has also gotten an upgrade for the latest advanced HDR format, Dolby Vision 2, making it well-primed for the future. It’s all wrapped in a stylish design, for a posh taste of next-gen luxury at an accessible price point.

It has been revealed that TCL was so confident in its entry-level QM6K that it was the first TV the brand released with its upcoming mini-LED display tech in 2025, and the only major model that wasn’t replaced for 2026. That badge of honor is well earned, as the QM6K is one of the best-performing TVs I’ve tested in its price class, with naturalistic colors, rich black levels and contrast, and enough brightness to properly light up HDR scenes like a blazing sunset or a jet’s afterburners.

Industry observers note that maybe just as impressive are the concerns the QM6K avoids. While most TVs in its class readily reveal issues like screen aberrations on solid backgrounds, light bleed from bright images, and awful off-angle performance, the QM6K mostly stays clear of those pitfalls so you can simply enjoy the picture without distraction. My only real performance complaint is the TV’s particularly bad sound, but given that nearly all TVs I test are much better off with a soundbar or speaker system, that’s not a major surprise.

Industry observers note that when it comes to extras, the QM6K is well stocked with options like VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) at up to 144 Hz for blur-free action and a gaming bar to adjust features on the fly. And while the TV isn’t nearly as bright as my top budget pick, the U6SF Pro, its Google TV smart system is more intuitive and responsive for a better overall user experience. With a 55-inch model now available for under $500, the QM6K is tough to pass up.

Industry observers note that most TVs on this list are available from 55 inches to large-scale models at 98 inches or larger, and at increasingly reasonable price points. A big reason for that is, unlike OLED, mini-LED TVs are scalable at a relatively low cost, so screens fit for large home theaters are much more attainable. That’s one of mini-LED’s biggest advantages over other display tech, not to mention the potential for next-gen brightness and color coverage at lower pricing. That noted, ultra-large screens more readily expose performance issues, so it’s important to balance screen size with quality so you don’t regret your purchase later.

All of the TVs on this list offer 4K resolution with HDR (High Dynamic Range), and you wouldn’t want to buy a TV with lower resolution these days unless you’re looking for a very small screen (around 48 inches or lower) for a bedroom or office. The majority of newly introduced content is shot in 4K with HDR, the latter of which provides higher brightness and better contrast between the lightest and darkest images, along with the potential for more vibrant colors. Some TVs still offer 8K resolution, but because 8K content is scarce and difficult to recognize with the naked eye, it’s essentially dead (or at least dormant) in the current TV landscape.

Sources indicate that as for refresh rates, any TV with 120-Hz or higher is preferred for fast-moving content like sports and, especially, gaming. All of the TVs on this list offer 120 Hz refresh rates or higher with VRR (Variable Refresh Rate), designed to adjust to games dynamically to reduce lag and screen tearing/blur. Many TVs push to 144 Hz or better, but those refresh rates are only accessible with select gaming PCs. For consoles—PS5, Xbox Series S/X, and the Nintendo Switch 2—120 Hz is sufficient.

All of the displays on this list use mini-LED-backlighting, a smaller and more accurate version of traditional LED backlighting, paired with a liquid-crystal display (LCD). Because mini-LEDs are smaller, they can be used more prevalently to create better brightness and more dimming zones, which can enhance black levels for better contrast between the brightest and darkest images. Mini-LEDs can also be enhanced by features like quantum dots, nanoparticles that produce pure bright colors when exposed to light. Some advanced Mini-LED TVs also use RGB LED technology, which trades uniform blue or white mini-LEDs for multicolor red, green, and blue light clusters designed to produce purer, more expansive colors at the light source.

In contrast (no pun intended), OLED displays use organic material excited by electricity to light each of a TV’s millions of pixels independently. These self-lit (a.k.a. self-emissive) displays have distinct advantages, including the ability to create perfect black levels for enhanced contrast over backlit displays, along with much wider viewing angles. Like mini-LEDs, some OLED displays also use quantum dots: So-called “QD-OLED” TVs offer enhanced brightness and colors, among other upcoming technologies to compete with ever-brighter and more advanced mini-LED TVs.

Both display types have their advantages. OLED is the best choice for those after a more balanced, nuanced, and uniform picture, especially if money isn’t a concern. However, because mini-LED is generally cheaper to produce, it may be a better choice for those on a budget who want the largest and brightest screen for their money. And in recent years, the best mini-LED TVs have increasingly advanced to better compete against OLED.

Sources indicate that the most important connectivity option for gamers is HDMI 2.1, which offers higher bandwidth to get the most out of gaming devices. HDMI 2.1 allows for high refresh rates and features like VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) from devices like the PS5, Xbox Series X, and gaming PCs. If you’re only connecting a Blu-ray player or streaming device, HDMI 2.0 will suffice. All of the TVs on this list also support HDMI eARC/ARC, which allows you to easily connect newer soundbars and other audio devices at high resolution for enhanced audio performance.

Industry observers note that wiFi 6 or 7 may also be helpful for wireless streaming, especially if you’re watching a lot of high-resolution content, though you’ll need a router that supports those formats. Most TVs also include an Ethernet connection for a mainline connection to your modem. Other connection options to consider include Bluetooth for connecting wireless headphones, ATSC 3.0 for features like over-the-air HDR from an HD antenna, and an optical connection for older audio devices like a legacy amplifier or soundbar.

According to recent reports, all the TVs on this list come with a smart TV platform for streaming from popular apps, and many include options that let you stream content directly from a smartphone like Apple AirPlay or Google Cast. My favorite platforms are Roku and Google TV, which I find the easiest to navigate and use on a daily basis. All smart platforms collect some form of personal information, so it’s notable to be careful when agreeing to terms and licensing to protect your privacy.

Each TV also supports multiple HDR formats, which is important for getting the best performance. HDR10 is the baseline format, which all modern TVs support. Most TVs also support dynamic HDR formats like Dolby Vision and HDR10+ (many support both). These advanced formats can provide a more precise vision of a director’s intent by adjusting the brightest and darkest images scene by scene, and even frame by frame. Dolby Vision is the most common dynamic HDR format for streaming.

Industry observers note that if you’re interested in voice control, you’ll want to look for voice assistants like Roku Voice, Amazon Alexa or Alexa+, and Google Assistant or Gemini. If you’re connecting an audio device that supports spatial audio, like a Dolby Atmos soundbar or A/V receiver, you may also want to ensure your TV supports 3D audio formats like Dolby Atmos and, for 4K Blu-rays, DTS:X.

Deadline looms for post-9/11 FirstNet reauthorization

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (960 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that in an aerial view, a fire truck sits parked in a neighborhood destroyed by a wildfire on Aug.
  • Supporters of the FirstNet program that provides emergency communications for first-responders still see hope for reauthorization this year, despite continued disagreements over what changes, if any, should be made to how the program is governed.
  • A House-passed reauthorization bill would shift authority toward the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and away from the FirstNet board, which is made up in part by first-responders.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that in an aerial view, a fire truck sits parked in a neighborhood destroyed by a wildfire on Aug. 11, 2023 in Lahaina, Hawaii. The performance of the FirstNet network during the Maui fires has partially led to calls for a revamp of its structure. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images).

Supporters of the FirstNet program that provides emergency communications for first-responders still see hope for reauthorization this year, despite continued disagreements over what changes, if any, should be made to how the program is governed.

A House-passed reauthorization bill would shift authority toward the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and away from the FirstNet board, which is made up in part by first-responders.

The potential change is opposed by the influential Fraternal Order of Police, but any fresh bill or amendment would require floor votes in both the House and Senate, a potentially tall order as the 119th Congress draws to a close.

Authority for FirstNet, a program developed in the wake of 9/11, is set to expire in February of 2027 unless lawmakers pass an extension.

The program’s governing entity, the First Responder Network Authority, was created in 2012 in response to recommendations after the terrorist attacks, during which public safety agencies using different radio systems and overloaded phone lines struggled to adequately communicate.

The House passed its bipartisan reauthorization bill in April via voice vote. Senators have not yet taken up that legislation or introduced their own. In January, the Senate Commerce Committee’s Telecommunications and Media Subcommittee held a hearing on the program.

Related: First-responder network reauthorization advances.

Craig Wheeler, a spokesman for subcommittee Chair Deb Fischer, R-Neb., said in a statement this week that reauthorization is still a priority.

According to recent reports, “Sen. Fischer has been working closely with Chair Cruz on a bill and is having bipartisan discussions with Ranking Member Cantwell,” Wheeler said, referring to Sens. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Maria Cantwell, D-Wash.

“Moving a bill as soon as possible remains a top priority for Sen. Fischer, including getting it through both chambers and signed into law by President Trump.”.

The House bill would extend authority for FirstNet through fiscal 2037, stagger terms on the authority’s board and require five members of the board with public safety backgrounds, rather than three as needed under current law.

At concern in the reauthorization debate, in part, is control of the First Responder Network Authority.

The House bill would eliminate language in current law that established FirstNet as an “independent” authority within the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and would require the administration’s approval for most non-planning or emergency actions, though the bill was amended to include a list of actions the network can take without NTIA approval.

The changes are meant to respond to reports from the Commerce Department's Office of Inspector General that found that the AT&T-run service was not sufficiently available during the Maui wildfires in 2023 and that senior officials of the FirstNet Authority attempted to interfere with audits.

The Maui report noted the small number of FirstNet subscriptions among state and local first responders in the area and in an op-ed earlier this year, Maui Fire Chief Brad Ventura noted his department was “not using FirstNet devices” at the time of the fires but is now adopting them. He also supported reauthorization in the op-ed.

Related: First-responders network faced with calls for change.

But the shifting of control drew opposition from the Fraternal Order of Police, which prior to the bill’s committee markup urged its members to instead support a “clean reauthorization” of the program.

In a recent development, jim Pasco, executive director of the FOP, emphasized his group’s desire to see decisions made by the FirstNet board, rather than by NTIA. He said that moving authority away from a group that is required to include first-responders would be “a threat to officer and public safety.”.

Yucel Ors, legislative director for public safety and crime prevention at the National League of Cities, said that his group, along with the International Association of Fire Chiefs and other state and local government and public safety groups, worked closely with the House, including on the changes to put some “everyday controls and functions” back directly under the board’s control.

He said the National League of Cities supported the House bill, but that they hope that any changes made to FirstNet’s governance are “not going to impact the day-to-day operations that public safety depend on, rely on, and expect.”.

Ors noted he expects the Senate would make changes to the House-passed bill, but he doesn’t know if those changes would come in the form of an amendment or an entirely new bill.

No proposed Senate amendment to the House bill, or alternative Senate bill, has yet to emerge.

He expressed concern over the timeline for reauthorization, especially if the Senate doesn’t take up the House bill as is.

A new Senate bill or amendment would require votes in both the House and Senate, with floor time dwindling as both chambers work through must-pass legislation before the end of the year.

Congress could potentially pass a short-term reauthorization of FirstNet. Ors expressed worry that option could jeopardize the public-private relationship with contractor AT&T.

Pasco remarked he would prefer a short reauthorization over the House-passed bill, but said he hopes a full reauthorization could still pass this Congress.

The House bill has strong bipartisan support and the Senate’s negotiations are also bipartisan. Both Ors and Pasco expressed confidence that if time runs out this year for a reauthorization bill, a new version of the legislation would still have strong prospects under a Democratic Congress.

Additional context regarding the role of FirstNet during the Maui fires was added to this report.

Latest Update: Do You Trust Your Own Intuition? Here’s How You Sharpen It—And Win at Life, Researchers Say

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.

It has been revealed that think about the phrase “it’s just like riding a bicycle.” At first, it’s hard, and you have to pay attention to what you’re doing, but after you’ve practiced for many hours, bike riding becomes so natural you don’t even have to think about it; you just hop on and go. In fact, you can hardly explain how you learned in the first place or exactly how you’re keeping your balance as you pedal on. You just trust your body to do it. The same applies to cognitive activities: As a child, you had to really think about how to arrive at the answer of 2+2, but now, you just know it’s four, without thinking.

Sources indicate that intuition is about finding the solution automatically and without deep thought, claims Wim De Neys, a cognitive psychologist and CNRS research professor at the University of Paris. At its core, your intuition is a behavior your brain develops based on patterns and experiences over time, a kind of automation for something you’ve done countless times. That’s why intuition is often linked to expertise. Trusting your gut may sound ill-advised, so why wouldn’t you want to think things through? But it turns out that generating your instincts for decision-making can both help you make the right choice in times of confusion and stress, and also free up mental resources for other tasks.

So, can you train your intuition to sense better choices?

According to recent reports, well, it’s not that simple, according to De Neys, whose research focuses on how intuitive and deliberate thinking develops over our lifetimes. You can’t sidestep the deep reflection needed to build the foundation of your intuitions. But you can tap into them in a more meaningful way, especially over time.

“Having gut feelings and intuition and even valid intuitions, there’s science to back it up,” De Neys states. “It exists, but it’s always tied to expertise, and expertise means it’s something that you’ve done a lot.”.

Intuition isn’t some overall sense; instead it’s tied to one area of expertise, like an interviewer being able to pick up on the candidate who’ll be the right fit for the job, or an experienced doctor delivering a diagnosis. While you won’t have expert intuition about everything under the sun, there are a few ways you can boost your own decision-making.

First, you need to get better at pattern matching, and that means practice. Intuition is tied to pattern-matching, Jeff Larsen, PhD, a professor of psychology at the University of Tennessee, explains. For example, chess masters earn their distinction by practicing so much that when they see the board, they don’t have to stop and think about what the two or three best moves will be. Others with less expertise may watch a game and think, “that was a silly move,” but they don’t realize the master player has spent years building up pattern recognition, or an accurate gut feeling, Larsen explains.

Sources indicate that second, stop second-guessing your intuition. You can do this by asking yourself, “How might I be wrong?” One approach is to ask a friend who may disagree with you or might have an outside perspective. This can also help you understand that, often, an instinctual choice you made in the heat of the moment is correct. Even if the choice isn’t exactly right, it’s probably good enough to keep you safe. For example, when you’re driving down the interstate, you have some intuition about whether you can make a lane change or not, and whether you need to slow down or speed up to avoid an accident. Thinking about the consequences of your decision-making can also help give you more confidence in your intuition.

Sometimes you have to trust your gut on a truly life-changing decision. When it comes to marriage, the information overload can sometimes feel overwhelming. However, when it comes to close relationships, you’ve presumably experienced many behavioral exchanges with your partner, and this allows for substantial information-gathering to “feed your gut,” Michael Olson, PhD, a professor of psychology at the University of Tennessee, explains.

Since you can’t possibly keep this massive load of information in your conscious memory at all times, it translates into a neat summary of all those behavioral exchanges. Now you have a gut feeling that this person is right for you—or not.

In a recent development, and the research agrees. A study Olson coauthored, published in Science, found that the “explicit,” or “conscious” evaluations couples in the study made of their partners while in the so-called initial “honeymoon stage” didn’t mean as much when stretched over four years. Instead, those who reported positive gut feelings over this time period had a more accurate idea of their happiness in their relationship.

Sources indicate that your gut doesn’t just extend to your love life. Trusting it can also help you to be successful in business. Elizabeth Rea, an evidentiary clairvoyant psychic medium, now teaches established founders and CEOs to tap into their own intuitions, through her company, Insightful. As a medium, Rea has also assisted U.S. federal special agents investigating cold murder cases.

Industry observers note that when working with clients, she asks them to relax what they consciously believe. Sometimes so-called gut feelings may come to us in the form of chills down our spine or another physical sensation. But since we’re living in a left-brained culture that prizes making decisions using logic and analysis, those instincts often get passed off as coincidences and ignored, Rea states. Sometimes, gut feelings may also be ignored because of self-doubt. Your intuition often whispers to you, she tells clients. Honing these signals will help you improve your self-trust—thereby improving your intuition.

Overall, training yourself to trust your intuition will help you become a better decision-maker. You’ll make the right choices without the agonizing process of picking through pros and cons and running scenarios in your brain for days on end.

“It’s a lot more cost-efficient if we can offload [decision-making] to our intuition,” De Neys says. “Often that’s going to be helpful because then it frees up resources for something else that might be more important at that point in time.”.
